## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |

  </priority_instructions>

       - Primary research tool. Runs commands in parallel, auto-indexes each output, and (when queries are passed) returns matching sections in the same round trip — no follow-up search call.
       - Each command: {label: "section header", command: "shell command"}; the label becomes the FTS5 chunk title — descriptive labels improve search.

       - Multiple related questions about anything already indexed (your captures + session memory). Batch every question in one array; the ranking pipeline runs per-query and the round-trip cost is paid once.
    3. PROCESSING: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute(language, code) | mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file(path, language, code)
       - Derive answers FROM data: filter, count, aggregate, parse, transform. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation; the raw bytes stay in the sandbox.

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

1	# Handoff — ATH Technology / Software Management Framework
2	
3	**Date:** 2026-08-12
4	**Owner:** Eric Rash (Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics)
5	**Status:** Delivered. Meeting 2026-08-13, 4:15–4:45 PM Central, Microsoft Teams —
6	"INITIAL DISCUSSION: ATH Technology/Software Review". Email sent by Eric himself.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## What this was
11	
12	Merge Eric's existing Software and Technology Management Framework draft with a
13	Baylor-format policy draft ("Responsible Use of Athlete Performance Technologies
14	and Data Policy", `JA_TechPolicy.pdf`, a 10-page scanned PDF with no text layer —
15	had to be OCR'd by rendering pages to PNG and reading them).
16	
17	Then condense into an executive summary plus a standalone workflow document, for
18	distribution ahead of the 8/13 meeting.
19	
20	## Merge specification (from Eric, after his meeting with Kenny Boyd)
21	
22	- Eric's document is the **skeleton**; JA sections merge into it.
23	- JA sections **1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8** come in. JA **5, 7, 9, 10, 11** and all
24	  appendices are **excluded**.
25	- JA §8 (Responsibilities) merges into **our §5 Roles** — this pinned Roles at §5,
26	  which forced JA 1–4 to fold *into* our existing §1–4 rather than sit ahead of them.
27	- The three-phase process moves to **last** (§8), followed by the workflow diagram (§9).
28	- Scope: **department-wide**, all Athletics technology, with athlete performance
29	  technology as the originating context and highest-risk category.
30	- Base file was the **Aug 11** draft (`..._DRAFT_ER_.docx`), which had §8.2
31	  trials/pilots deleted and a newer diagram. Eric confirmed §8.2 stays out.
32	
33	**Trap that nearly caused an error:** three near-identical drafts existed in
34	`deliverables/`. The *newest* (Aug 11) had FEWER sections than the Aug 7 file Eric
35	originally pointed at. Always diff before choosing a base.
36	
37	## Final section structure
38	
39	| § | Section | Source |
40	|---|---|---|
41	| 1 | Purpose | Eric + JA 1 Policy Statement (1.1) + JA 2 Reason (1.2) |
42	| 2 | Scope and terminology | Eric + JA 3 (2.2) + JA 4 (2.3) + JA 6 Definitions (2.4) |
43	| 3 | Alignment with NCAA guidance | Eric, unchanged |
44	| 4 | Intended outcomes | Eric |
45	| 5 | Roles and responsibilities | Eric's 7 roles + JA's 6 = 13 |
46	| 6 | Levels of review | Eric, retitled + relabeled |
47	| 7 | Exceptions | Eric |
48	| 8 | The three phases | Eric, moved last |
49	| 9 | Workflow | diagram |
50	
51	## Decisions made (and the reasoning that would otherwise be lost)
52	
53	1. **Review tiers renamed.** Kenny rejected Light/Standard/Elevated. He floated
54	   Basic/Intermediate/Advanced; that was **declined** because it reads as
55	   sophistication of the *technology* rather than depth of *review*, and "Basic"
56	   sounds like a judgment on the requester. Shipped
57	   **Level 1 Standard / Level 2 Enhanced / Level 3 Comprehensive Review**, section
58	   retitled "Levels of review". **This is a proposal, not a settled decision.**
59	
60	2. **ITS seniority framing.** Kenny wanted a supervisory-level IT person, not a line
61	   technician. Written as what the *request* demands ("ITS is represented at a
62	   supervisory level with the authority to commit ITS resources"), never as a
63	   competence judgment on staff.
64	
65	3. **No blame-implying rationale.** "so the department stops discovering it is in
66	   the final year of an agreement with no time to act" → "advance visibility of
67	   contract end dates and the lead time to evaluate options". See Tier A memory
68	   `project_kenny-boyd-doc-review-preferences.md`.
69	
70	4. **Urgency gate.** A request directed by an administrative lead enters the
71	   expedited lane on receipt — a documented gate instead of arguing case by case.
72	
73	5. **Humanizer: narrow pass only.** Ran 9 edits on sentences Claude authored.
74	   Deliberately did NOT touch Eric's own language or JA's policy text, and ignored
75	   the skill's "add soul / use first person / let some mess in" half, which is blog
76	   advice that would damage a policy document headed to OGC.
77	
78	6. **Diagram "tier" → "level".** The workflow PNG said "tier" twice, contradicting
79	   the new §6. Re-rendered both labels in the original Cascadia Code at matched size
80	   and centering (48px, 3× export scale, 10px padding — geometry recovered exactly
81	   from the .excalidraw JSON). Pixel-faithful. "level" survives whatever naming
82	   Kenny finally picks.
83	
84	7. **Eric's own edit pass (8/12, in OneDrive)** — 9 changes, all honored:
85	   cut "No single unit can make that call alone"; "carries"→"handles the most
86	   sensitive data"; "depends on what it actually involves"→"the request's scope";
87	   **cut "The framework is department-wide … any single unit"**; "the deepest
88	   review"→"a review"; cut "defaulting on whatever is asked for"; cut the §6
89	   re-levelling sentences; cut "not a bypass" / "compressed clock" and reworded the
90	   urgency gate; tightened 1.7 and expanded "Dir App"→"Director of Applied".
91	
92	## File locations
93	
94	**Local — `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework/deliverables/`**
95	- `Software_and_Tech_Management_MERGED_ER_2026-08-12.docx` / `.pdf` — framework (7pp)
96	- `Software_and_Tech_Management_EXEC_SUMMARY_ER_2026-08-12.docx` / `.pdf` (2pp)
97	- `Software_and_Tech_Management_WORKFLOW_ER_2026-08-12.docx` / `.pdf` (3pp)
98	- `Software_and_Tech_Management_MERGED_ER_2026-08-12_SUPERSEDED_pre-edit.docx` — old build, kept
99	- `Framework_level-language.excalidraw` — diagram source with "level" wording
100	- `Workflow_Diagram_level-language.png` — the corrected diagram
101	- `Framework.excalidraw` — ORIGINAL, untouched, still says "tier"
102	- 08-11 versions of all three documents also retained
103	
104	**OneDrive — `/Users/kristinarash/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-BaylorUniversity/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/XXXX_Transfer/SoftwareTechDocs/`**
105	- Same five shared files, byte-identical (SHA-256 verified)
106	- Plus `Software_and_Tech_Management_2026-08-12.pdf` (Eric's own export; note the
107	  filename lacks the role token the others carry)
108	
109	**Build scripts — `~/.claude/jobs/126c5de4/tmp/`** (ephemeral, dies with the job)
110	`baylordoc.py` (shared styling), `build_merged.py`, `build_exec.py`,
111	`build_workflow.py`, `patch_diagram.py`, `extract_full.py`, `topdf4.scpt`.
112	`build_merged.py` now writes to `..._MERGED_ER_REBUILD_DO-NOT-SEND.docx` so a rerun
113	cannot overwrite Eric's edited framework. **If these scripts matter beyond this job,
114	copy them somewhere durable.**
115	
116	## Gotchas for whoever picks this up
117	
118	- **OneDrive is the source of truth.** Eric edits there. The local copy is a
119	  snapshot and goes stale silently — nothing keeps them in sync.
120	- **Never rerun `build_merged.py` against the canonical filename.** It would wipe
121	  Eric's edits with no warning.
122	- **Word automation is flaky.** `active document` returns empty right after `open`;
123	  needs a wait loop (`topdf4.scpt`). When it wedges, a full quit + relaunch fixes it —
124	  killing it is safe only when `count of documents` is 0.
125	- No LibreOffice / Pages / pandoc on this machine. Word is the only DOCX→PDF path.
126	- The `gws` CLI is authed to **personal** Gmail (eric.rash11@gmail.com), not Baylor.
127	  Contacts API returns 403 (missing scope). Calendar work events come from a
128	  read-only subscribed feed that strips attendees.
129	
130	## Next actions
131	
132	1. **8/13 meeting** — two open questions to land: the Level 1/2/3 naming, and the
133	   scope wording. Eric's edit removed "department-wide" from §2.1, which was the
134	   specific thing Kenny asked to strengthen; §1.2 still carries the idea
135	   ("the department's general approach to all technology") but that §2.1 sentence is
136	   where a challenge will land.
137	2. **After naming is settled** — update `Framework_level-language.excalidraw` and
138	   re-export the PNG, then rebuild the workflow doc.
139	3. Consider archiving the 08-11 document set to cut folder clutter.

BAYLOR ATHLETICS
Software and Technology Management Framework
Executive Summary
Status
Draft for discussion
Date
August 12, 2026
Prepared by
Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Companion documents
Software and Technology Management Framework (full); Request Workflow; Technology Idea Form; Internal ATH Form; Technology Evaluation Scorecard; Request Tracker

In brief
Requests for software and technology currently move through different channels depending on who initiates them. This framework establishes one route for every request: a single intake, two control points in a fixed order, a named point of contact, a review depth matched to the request's scope, and a scheduled decision on whether to renew.
It applies to technology requests in the department and covers all software and technology. Athlete performance technology sits within that scope as the category that handles sensitive data.
Why this framework
Technology used in athletics can collect biometric, health-related, performance, workload, recovery, video, sensor, and survey data. Responsible use requires coordination across Athletics, Sports Medicine, ITS, Privacy, Legal, Compliance, Procurement, and Records Management.
The NCAA Sports Science Institute has published guidance on the responsible use of performance technologies. That guidance is high-level by design and leaves implementation to each school. This framework is Baylor Athletics' implementation.
The department needs a shared view of what it already owns, when agreements end, and the utilization of purchased technology.
What it establishes
One intake covers every request: the Technology Idea Form and the internal ATH Form, which declare the data category and the proposed review level at intake.
Two control points, in order. The Business Office reviews budget, contract, and duplication; ITS then reviews technical, security, and integration. A request is purchased only after both have cleared it, and declined requests come back with documented reasons.
One point of contact. The Director of Applied Performance facilitates, holds a weekly standing meeting with ITS on all open requests, and provides regular updates on the status of any open request. Requesters are brought in when needed; standing attendance is not expected.
Review depth that scales. Three levels, from a compliance and privacy check through to full review with Health & Wellness and medical sign-off.
A scheduled decision. Every product is reviewed at six months or the end of the competitive season, whichever is longer. The outcome is to renew, renegotiate, or discontinue.
How a request moves
Phase
What happens
Who owns it
Phase 1Proposal, approval,purchase
Intake forms completed and the review level declared. Business Office reviews, then ITS. The request is scored against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard and purchased only after both control points are cleared.
Requester initiates; Business Office and ITS are the control points
Phase 2Implementation andproduct use
A project manager is assigned. The weekly ITS standing meeting tracks every open request, so each one has a known owner and a known blocker.
Assigned Project Manager, facilitated by the Director of Applied Performance
Phase 3Review andrenewal decision
Utilization is compared against the intent stated on the original request.
Sport Administrator signs off

How deeply a request is reviewed
Level
Applies when
Review includes
Level 1Standard Review
No athlete data; single unit; low or one-time cost
Compliance, Privacy, Ownership, Transparency, Interoperability
Level 2Enhanced Review
Performance data, multi-team use, or recurring cost
Full review
Level 3Comprehensive Review
Physiological or health data; external data sharing; third-party processing of athlete data
Full review, plus data protection review and Health & Wellness / medical sign-off

Exceptions
Urgent requests clear the same two control points, with a short risk checklist completed at intake. A request directed by an administrative lead enters the expedited lane on receipt, which provides documentation for what qualifies as urgent, so the distinction does not have to be determined on a case-by-case basis.

content.content:
1. Purpose
To increase the efficiency and timeliness of requests for software and technology purchase and implementation, and to establish a consistent, transparent process for how those decisions are made, reviewed, and renewed.
1.1  Policy statement
Baylor Athletics shall select, acquire, implement, use, access, disclose, retain, and dispose of software, technology, and the data they generate only for authorized athletics, sports medicine, health, safety, performance, compliance, and operational purposes, and only in accordance with Baylor University policies, applicable law, NCAA guidance, contractual obligations, and approved data-governance practices.
Software and technology must be governed through a written plan, routine education, defined data rights, structured technology review, and continuous improvement.
1.2  Reason for the framework
Technology used in athletics may collect biometric, health-related, performance, workload, recovery, video, sensor, survey, software, mobile-application, and other individual-level data. Responsible use of these technologies requires coordination across Athletics, Sports Medicine, Information Technology Services, Privacy, Legal, Compliance, Procurement, and Records Management.
This framework is intended to help Baylor Athletics support student-athlete health, safety, privacy, autonomy, data security, and performance while reducing legal, regulatory, contractual, operational, and reputational risk.
The framework started with athlete performance technology, which handles the most sensitive data and is subject to the clearest NCAA guidance. It is written to serve as the department's general approach to all technology. The process below applies to every technology request in the department, and the depth of review depends on the request's scope.
2. Scope and terminology
2.1  Scope
Technology refers to tangible items like devices, wearables, equipment, and applications. Software refers to the platforms and systems those items connect to. The two are rarely purchased independently, and this framework covers both.
The framework is not limited to performance, health, and wellness. Athlete performance technology sits inside that scope and triggers a review. A request that does not involve any athlete data still goes through the same review mechanism.
2.2  Individuals and entities affected
Baylor Athletics staff, coaches, sports medicine personnel, strength and conditioning staff, analysts, administrators, student support staff, and other Baylor personnel who select, use, access, interpret, or disclose technology and the data it generates.
Student-athletes whose data is collected, used, analyzed, inferred, stored, or disclosed through these technologies.
Vendors, contractors, consultants, and other third parties that collect, store, process, analyze, host, transmit, or receive Baylor Athletics data on Baylor's behalf.
Baylor units supporting Athletics, including ITS, Information Security, Office of General Counsel, University Compliance and Risk Services, Privacy, Internal Audit, Procurement, and records-management functions.
2.3  Exclusions
This framework does not replace or supersede Baylor policies that already govern specific categories of data, systems, conduct, records, or legal obligations. Where a more specific Baylor policy applies, that policy continues to govern. This document should be read as an Athletics-specific overlay that routes technology decisions into existing Baylor governance channels rather than around them.
2.4  Definitions
Term
Definition for this framework
Technology
Tangible items such as devices, wearables, sensors, cameras, and equipment, together with the applications that operate them.
Software
The platforms and systems that technology connects to, including hosted, cloud, and on-premises applications.
Athlete Performance Technology
Any device, sensor, wearable, software, mobile application, camera, survey, analytics platform, AI-enabled system, or other technology used to collect, infer, monitor, analyze, store, or communicate biometric, performance, workload, recovery, wellness, health, safety, training, competition, or related data about student-athletes.
Athlete Performance Technology Data
Data collected, generated, inferred, stored, analyzed, or disclosed through athlete performance technologies, including performance metrics, physiological metrics, sleep, hydration, nutrition, stress indicators, recovery, training load, practice or game analytics, and related data.
Restricted / Protected Data
Data subject to Baylor data-classification requirements and heightened safeguards, including where applicable PHI, FERPA records, biometric identifiers, credentials, SSNs, financial information, IRB-related research data, and other regulated or sensitive data.
Medical Decision-Making Data
Data used, intended to be used, or reasonably likely to be used to inform medical management, injury evaluation, treatment, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions.
Approved Use Case
A documented and approved purpose, user population, data category, vendor or system, and data lifecycle for a technology.
Student-Athlete Notice
A plain-language explanation to student-athletes of what data is collected, why, who may access it, permissible uses, retention, rights, questions, and concerns.
1.1  A request is initiated by the Director of Applied Performance, a Head Coach, or any Admin Unit Director.
1.2  The requester completes the Technology Idea Form and the internal ATH Form. The request must declare its data category and proposed review level.
1.3  The request goes to the Business Office. The Business Office serves as the filter for all requests and the first control point.
1.4  The forms are submitted to ITS for technical, security, and integration review. This is the second control point.
1.5  The request is evaluated against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard.
1.6  A request is disseminated for purchase only after clearing both control points. Declined requests are returned with documented reasons.
1.7  The Director of Applied Performance holds a weekly standing meeting with the ITS representative to review the status of all open requests across all units. The requester may be brought into the meeting where input is needed; their standing attendance is not expected. The Director of Applied Performance provides regular updates on the status of any open request.
Phase 2 — Implementation and Product Use
2.1  A project manager is assigned. This may be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied, depending on the unit and the system.
2.2  Status flows from the weekly ITS standing meeting through the Director of Applied to the assigned project manager and stakeholders, so that every open request has a known owner.
2.3  Open requests are tracked as follows: project, item, requester, project manager, date submitted, desired implementation date, current status, and what is holding it up.
Phase 3 — Product Review and Renewal Decision

# Talking Points — INITIAL DISCUSSION: ATH Technology/Software Review

**Meeting:** Thu 2026-08-13, 4:15–4:45 PM Central, MS Teams
**Prepared for:** Eric Rash — internal prep only, not for distribution
**Companion:** Executive Summary (2pp) already circulated; this is what the summary
deliberately does *not* say.

Filter used: every point below requires someone else in the room to **agree, decide,
or commit a resource**. Anything that only describes what the framework does is
already in the summary and was cut.

---

## 1. The review-level names are a proposal, and two other things are waiting on them

**Say:** "Level 1 Standard / Level 2 Enhanced / Level 3 Comprehensive is a proposal,
not a decision. I'd like to land the naming today because the workflow diagram and
the workflow document both carry that language."

**Context you hold:** Light/Standard/Elevated was rejected. Basic/Intermediate/
Advanced was floated and set aside because it reads as sophistication of the
*technology* rather than depth of *review* — and "Basic" lands as a judgment on the
person making the request. The current set describes review depth without grading the
requester.

**What you want out of the room:** a naming decision, or an explicit "we'll live with
these for now." Either ends the loop. The diagram is already re-rendered in neutral
"level" wording, so it survives whatever gets picked — but it can't be finalized
until someone picks.

---

## 2. Scope: the framework is department-wide, and here is the sentence that says so

**Say:** "This covers all Athletics technology. Athlete performance technology is
where it started and it's the highest-risk category, but a request with no athlete
data goes through the same route."

**The sentences to point at if pressed** — you don't need to open the document, but
know where they live:

- **§1.2** — "The process below applies to every technology request in the
  department, and the depth of review depends on the request's scope."
- **§2.1** — "The framework is not limited to performance, health, and wellness…
  A request that does not involve any athlete data still goes through the same
  review mechanism."

**Why this is on the list:** this is the point most likely to be challenged, and the
phrase "department-wide" itself no longer appears in §2.1 after the last edit pass.
The *idea* is fully carried by the two sentences above — the label is what's gone.
If someone wants the words back, that's a one-line change, not a rewrite. Don't
concede scope; concede wording.

---

## 3. Nothing in the framework creates the inventory of what we already own

This is the real gap, and an initial discussion is the right place to raise it.

- **§4 Intended outcomes** promises "a consistent, shared understanding of the entire
  inventory of software and technology in use across the department."
- **Phase 3** reviews utilization "against the intent stated on the original request."

Those only connect for technology that came in *through* the framework. Everything
the department bought before today has no request to compare against, no owner, and
no renewal date on anyone's calendar. The Request Tracker exists as a file; no one
is assigned to populate it with what's already in use.

**Say:** "The renewal gate works going forward. It doesn't tell us what we're already
paying for or when those agreements end. Who owns building that baseline, and by
when?"

**What you want out of the room:** a name and a date. If neither is available today,
get agreement that it's a known gap and a follow-up item — that alone protects you
from owning it by default.

---

## If it comes up

- **The framework commits other departments' time.** Two control points in fixed
  order — Business Office, then ITS — with nothing purchased until both clear. Plus
  ITS represented at a supervisory level with authority to commit ITS resources, plus
  a weekly standing meeting. That's a recurring ask of ITS. If ITS is in the room,
  expect this to be where friction shows up, and the framing is what the *request*
  demands, never a comment on staffing. **The change worth naming out loud: this
  moves "who can say no" into a documented order.**

- **Does this become policy?** Right now it's an Athletics-specific overlay that
  routes into existing Baylor governance rather than around it (§2.3). Whether it
  needs an OGC/University policy path to carry weight is a genuine open question —
  worth raising if there's time, but it's the first thing to drop from a 30-minute
  agenda.

- **Urgency gate — settled, don't re-open.** A request directed by an administrative
  lead enters the expedited lane on receipt, and still clears both control points. It
  is documented specifically so it isn't argued case by case.

---

## Two questions to leave with

1. Are the Level 1/2/3 names final enough to build the diagram on?
2. Who owns the baseline inventory of technology already in use, and by when?

1	
2	BAYLOR ATHLETICS
3	Software and Technology Management Framework
4	Status
5	Draft for discussion
6	Date
7	August 12, 2026
8	Prepared by
9	Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
10	Responsible offices
11	Intercollegiate Athletics; Information Technology Services; Office of General Counsel; University Compliance and Risk Services
12	Review and approval
13	Business Office and ITS serve as the two control points. Final policy language should be reviewed by the Office of General Counsel, University Compliance and Risk Services, ITS, and Privacy.
14	
15	1. Purpose
16	To increase the efficiency and timeliness of requests for software and technology purchase and implementation, and to establish a consistent, transparent process for how those decisions are made, reviewed, and renewed.
17	1.1  Policy statement
18	Baylor Athletics shall select, acquire, implement, use, access, disclose, retain, and dispose of software, technology, and the data they generate only for authorized athletics, sports medicine, health, safety, performance, compliance, and operational purposes, and only in accordance with Baylor University policies, applicable law, NCAA guidance, contractual obligations, and approved data-governance practices.
19	Software and technology must be governed through a written plan, routine education, defined data rights, structured technology review, and continuous improvement.
20	1.2  Reason for the framework
21	Technology used in athletics may collect biometric, health-related, performance, workload, recovery, video, sensor, survey, software, mobile-application, and other individual-level data. Responsible use of these technologies requires coordination across Athletics, Sports Medicine, Information Technology Services, Privacy, Legal, Compliance, Procurement, and Records Management.
22	This framework is intended to help Baylor Athletics support student-athlete health, safety, privacy, autonomy, data security, and performance while reducing legal, regulatory, contractual, operational, and reputational risk.
23	The framework started with athlete performance technology, which handles the most sensitive data and is subject to the clearest NCAA guidance. It is written to serve as the department's general approach to all technology. The process below applies to every technology request in the department, and the depth of review depends on the request's scope.
24	2. Scope and terminology
25	2.1  Scope
26	Technology refers to tangible items like devices, wearables, equipment, and applications. Software refers to the platforms and systems those items connect to. The two are rarely purchased independently, and this framework covers both.
27	The framework is not limited to performance, health, and wellness. Athlete performance technology sits inside that scope and triggers a review. A request that does not involve any athlete data still goes through the same review mechanism.
28	2.2  Individuals and entities affected
29	Baylor Athletics staff, coaches, sports medicine personnel, strength and conditioning staff, analysts, administrators, student support staff, and other Baylor personnel who select, use, access, interpret, or disclose technology and the data it generates.
30	Student-athletes whose data is collected, used, analyzed, inferred, stored, or disclosed through these technologies.
31	Vendors, contractors, consultants, and other third parties that collect, store, process, analyze, host, transmit, or receive Baylor Athletics data on Baylor's behalf.
32	Baylor units supporting Athletics, including ITS, Information Security, Office of General Counsel, University Compliance and Risk Services, Privacy, Internal Audit, Procurement, and records-management functions.
33	2.3  Exclusions
34	This framework does not replace or supersede Baylor policies that already govern specific categories of data, systems, conduct, records, or legal obligations. Where a more specific Baylor policy applies, that policy continues to govern. This document should be read as an Athletics-specific overlay that routes technology decisions into existing Baylor governance channels rather than around them.
35	2.4  Definitions
36	Term
37	Definition for this framework
38	Technology
39	Tangible items such as devices, wearables, sensors, cameras, and equipment, together with the applications that operate them.
40	Software
41	The platforms and systems that technology connects to, including hosted, cloud, and on-premises applications.
42	Athlete Performance Technology
43	Any device, sensor, wearable, software, mobile application, camera, survey, analytics platform, AI-enabled system, or other technology used to collect, infer, monitor, analyze, store, or communicate biometric, performance, workload, recovery, wellness, health, safety, training, competition, or related data about student-athletes.
44	Athlete Performance Technology Data
45	Data collected, generated, inferred, stored, analyzed, or disclosed through athlete performance technologies, including performance metrics, physiological metrics, sleep, hydration, nutrition, stress indicators, recovery, training load, practice or game analytics, and related data.
46	Restricted / Protected Data
47	Data subject to Baylor data-classification requirements and heightened safeguards, including where applicable PHI, FERPA records, biometric identifiers, credentials, SSNs, financial information, IRB-related research data, and other regulated or sensitive data.
48	Medical Decision-Making Data
49	Data used, intended to be used, or reasonably likely to be used to inform medical management, injury evaluation, treatment, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions.
50	Approved Use Case
51	A documented and approved purpose, user population, data category, vendor or system, and data lifecycle for a technology.
52	Student-Athlete Notice
53	A plain-language explanation to student-athletes of what data is collected, why, who may access it, permissible uses, retention, rights, questions, and concerns.
54	
55	3. Alignment with NCAA guidance
56	The NCAA Sports Science Institute has published guidance on the Responsible Use of Performance Technologies in College Athletics. That guidance is high-level by design, leaving each school to implement it according to its own needs and resources. This framework is Baylor Athletics' implementation.
57	4. Intended outcomes
58	A consistent, shared understanding of the entire inventory of software and technology in use across the department.
59	Improved utilization of what the department already owns.
60	Coordinated renewal and term review, giving the department advance visibility of contract end dates and the lead time to evaluate options well before a renewal decision is due.
61	Increased staff fluency so that sport administrators and unit staff can address technology questions with confidence.
62	5. Roles and responsibilities
63	The roles below combine the operating roles that move a request through the process with the review functions that must be applied before a request can clear.
64	Role
65	Responsibility in this framework
66	Head Coach, Admin, and/or Unit Director
67	Initiates the request. Completes the Idea Form and internal ATH Form, including the declared data category and proposed review level.
68	Athletics Executive Sponsor
69	Owns Athletics operational compliance with this framework and ensures teams, coaches, and staff use approved technologies and approved use cases.
70	Business Office
71	First control point. Filters all requests before they proceed. Budget, contract, and duplication check process through the Business Office.
72	ITS / Information Security
73	Second control point. Technical, security, and integration review; confirms the system can be supported. Reviews access, authentication, storage, transmission, monitoring, incident response, and security controls. These requests carry integration, contract, and security implications across departments, so ITS is represented at a supervisory level with the authority to commit ITS resources and to decide on integration and security posture. Technical staff are brought in for specialist review as the request requires.
74	Director of Applied Performance
75	Single point of contact and facilitator. Holds the weekly standing meeting with ITS and relays status to project managers and stakeholders. Facilitator, not owner; not the subject-matter expert and not the project manager.
76	Assigned Project Manager
77	Owns delivery of the individual project. May be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied Performance.
78	Sport Administrator
79	Signs off on renewal decisions at Phase 3, informed by the usage review.
80	Health & Wellness / Sports Medicine
81	Reviews requests involving physiologic or health data. Must be involved where data may inform medical decision-making, injury evaluation, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions.
82	Athletics Compliance
83	Coordinates NCAA, conference, student-athlete, and departmental compliance implications.
84	Office of General Counsel / Privacy
85	Reviews FERPA, HIPAA, Texas privacy, consent, data rights, disclosure, vendor terms, and legal holds.
86	Procurement / Contracting
87	Ensures vendor contracts address ownership, permitted use, storage, access, data sharing, AI training, automated decision-making, downstream sharing, retention, deletion, portability, and breach notification.
88	Coaches, Staff, and Users
89	Use technology only for approved purposes, complete required training, avoid unauthorized disclosure, and report suspected misuse or incidents.
90	Student-Athlete Representatives
91	Provide feedback on transparency, education, perceived benefits, and potential unintended impacts of technology use.
92	
93	6. Levels of review
94	The level of review depends on three things: what data the technology touches, how many units it serves, and what the department is committing to in cost and contract term.
95	Level
96	Applies when
97	Review includes
98	Level 1Standard Review
99	No athlete data; single unit; low or one-time cost
100	Compliance, Privacy, Ownership, Transparency, Interoperability
101	Level 2Enhanced Review
102	Performance data, multi-team use, or recurring cost
103	Full review
104	Level 3Comprehensive Review
105	Physiologic or health data; external data sharing; third-party processing of athlete data
106	Full review, plus data protection review and Health & Wellness / medical sign-off
107	
108	The level is proposed by the requester at intake and confirmed at the control points.
109	7. Exceptions
110	7.1  Urgent and “emergency” requests
111	Urgent requests clear the same control points, with a short risk checklist completed at intake to surface issues that would otherwise delay the request: data category, contract term, integration dependency, and whether athlete data leaves Baylor.
112	A request directed by an administrative lead enters the expedited lane on receipt. This provides documentation for what qualifies as urgent, so the distinction does not have to be determined on a case-by-case basis at intake. An expedited request still clears both control points and still carries the review level its data and commitment call for.
113	8. The three phases
114	Phase 1 — Proposal, Approval, Purchase
115	1.1  A request is initiated by the Director of Applied Performance, a Head Coach, or any Admin Unit Director.
116	1.2  The requester completes the Technology Idea Form and the internal ATH Form. The request must declare its data category and proposed review level.
117	1.3  The request goes to the Business Office. The Business Office serves as the filter for all requests and the first control point.
118	1.4  The forms are submitted to ITS for technical, security, and integration review. This is the second control point.
119	1.5  The request is evaluated against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard.
120	1.6  A request is disseminated for purchase only after clearing both control points. Declined requests are returned with documented reasons.
121	1.7  The Director of Applied Performance holds a weekly standing meeting with the ITS representative to review the status of all open requests across all units. The requester may be brought into the meeting where input is needed; their standing attendance is not expected. The Director of Applied Performance provides regular updates on the status of any open request.
122	Phase 2 — Implementation and Product Use

BAYLOR ATHLETICS
Software and Technology Management Framework
Status
Draft for discussion
Date
August 12, 2026
Prepared by
Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Responsible offices
Intercollegiate Athletics; Information Technology Services; Office of General Counsel; University Compliance and Risk Services
Review and approval
Business Office and ITS serve as the two control points. Final policy language should be reviewed by the Office of General Counsel, University Compliance and Risk Services, ITS, and Privacy.

1. Purpose
To increase the efficiency and timeliness of requests for software and technology purchase and implementation, and to establish a consistent, transparent process for how those decisions are made, reviewed, and renewed.
1.1  Policy statement
Baylor Athletics shall select, acquire, implement, use, access, disclose, retain, and dispose of software, technology, and the data they generate only for authorized athletics, sports medicine, health, safety, performance, compliance, and operational purposes, and only in accordance with Baylor University policies, applicable law, NCAA guidance, contractual obligations, and approved data-governance practices.
Software and technology must be governed through a written plan, routine education, defined data rights, structured technology review, and continuous improvement.
1.2  Reason for the framework
Technology used in athletics may collect biometric, health-related, performance, workload, recovery, video, sensor, survey, software, mobile-application, and other individual-level data. Responsible use of these technologies requires coordination across Athletics, Sports Medicine, Information Technology Services, Privacy, Legal, Compliance, Procurement, and Records Management.
This framework is intended to help Baylor Athletics support student-athlete health, safety, privacy, autonomy, data security, and performance while reducing legal, regulatory, contractual, operational, and reputational risk.
The framework started with athlete performance technology, which handles the most sensitive data and is subject to the clearest NCAA guidance. It is written to serve as the department's general approach to all technology. The process below applies to every technology request in the department, and the depth of review depends on the request's scope.
2. Scope and terminology
2.1  Scope
Technology refers to tangible items like devices, wearables, equipment, and applications. Software refers to the platforms and systems those items connect to. The two are rarely purchased independently, and this framework covers both.
The framework is not limited to performance, health, and wellness. Athlete performance technology sits inside that scope and triggers a review. A request that does not involve any athlete data still goes through the same review mechanism.
2.2  Individuals and entities affected
Baylor Athletics staff, coaches, sports medicine personnel, strength and conditioning staff, analysts, administrators, student support staff, and other Baylor personnel who select, use, access, interpret, or disclose technology and the data it generates.
Student-athletes whose data is collected, used, analyzed, inferred, stored, or disclosed through these technologies.
Vendors, contractors, consultants, and other third parties that collect, store, process, analyze, host, transmit, or receive Baylor Athletics data on Baylor's behalf.
Baylor units supporting Athletics, including ITS, Information Security, Office of General Counsel, University Compliance and Risk Services, Privacy, Internal Audit, Procurement, and records-management functions.
2.3  Exclusions
This framework does not replace or supersede Baylor policies that already govern specific categories of data, systems, conduct, records, or legal obligations. Where a more specific Baylor policy applies, that policy continues to govern. This document should be read as an Athletics-specific overlay that routes technology decisions into existing Baylor governance channels rather than around them.
2.4  Definitions
Term
Definition for this framework
Technology
Tangible items such as devices, wearables, sensors, cameras, and equipment, together with the applications that operate them.
Software
The platforms and systems that technology connects to, including hosted, cloud, and on-premises applications.
Athlete Performance Technology
Any device, sensor, wearable, software, mobile application, camera, survey, analytics platform, AI-enabled system, or other technology used to collect, infer, monitor, analyze, store, or communicate biometric, performance, workload, recovery, wellness, health, safety, training, competition, or related data about student-athletes.
Athlete Performance Technology Data
Data collected, generated, inferred, stored, analyzed, or disclosed through athlete performance technologies, including performance metrics, physiological metrics, sleep, hydration, nutrition, stress indicators, recovery, training load, practice or game analytics, and related data.
Restricted / Protected Data
Data subject to Baylor data-classification requirements and heightened safeguards, including where applicable PHI, FERPA records, biometric identifiers, credentials, SSNs, financial information, IRB-related research data, and other regulated or sensitive data.
Medical Decision-Making Data
Data used, intended to be used, or reasonably likely to be used to inform medical management, injury evaluation, treatment, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions.
Approved Use Case
A documented and approved purpose, user population, data category, vendor or system, and data lifecycle for a technology.
Student-Athlete Notice
A plain-language explanation to student-athletes of what data is collected, why, who may access it, permissible uses, retention, rights, questions, and concerns.

3. Alignment with NCAA guidance
The NCAA Sports Science Institute has published guidance on the Responsible Use of Performance Technologies in College Athletics. That guidance is high-level by design, leaving each school to implement it according to its own needs and resources. This framework is Baylor Athletics' implementation.
4. Intended outcomes
A consistent, shared understanding of the entire inventory of software and technology in use across the department.
Improved utilization of what the department already owns.
Coordinated renewal and term review, giving the department advance visibility of contract end dates and the lead time to evaluate options well before a renewal decision is due.
Increased staff fluency so that sport administrators and unit staff can address technology questions with confidence.
5. Roles and responsibilities
The roles below combine the operating roles that move a request through the process with the review functions that must be applied before a request can clear.
Role
Responsibility in this framework
Head Coach, Admin, and/or Unit Director
Initiates the request. Completes the Idea Form and internal ATH Form, including the declared data category and proposed review level.
Athletics Executive Sponsor
Owns Athletics operational compliance with this framework and ensures teams, coaches, and staff use approved technologies and approved use cases.
Business Office
First control point. Filters all requests before they proceed. Budget, contract, and duplication check process through the Business Office.
ITS / Information Security
Second control point. Technical, security, and integration review; confirms the system can be supported. Reviews access, authentication, storage, transmission, monitoring, incident response, and security controls. These requests carry integration, contract, and security implications across departments, so ITS is represented at a supervisory level with the authority to commit ITS resources and to decide on integration and security posture. Technical staff are brought in for specialist review as the request requires.
Director of Applied Performance
Single point of contact and facilitator. Holds the weekly standing meeting with ITS and relays status to project managers and stakeholders. Facilitator, not owner; not the subject-matter expert and not the project manager.
Assigned Project Manager
Owns delivery of the individual project. May be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied Performance.
Sport Administrator
Signs off on renewal decisions at Phase 3, informed by the usage review.
Health & Wellness / Sports Medicine
Reviews requests involving physiologic or health data. Must be involved where data may inform medical decision-making, injury evaluation, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions.
Athletics Compliance
Coordinates NCAA, conference, student-athlete, and departmental compliance implications.
Office of General Counsel / Privacy
Reviews FERPA, HIPAA, Texas privacy, consent, data rights, disclosure, vendor terms, and legal holds.
Procurement / Contracting
Ensures vendor contracts address ownership, permitted use, storage, access, data sharing, AI training, automated decision-making, downstream sharing, retention, deletion, portability, and breach notification.
Coaches, Staff, and Users
Use technology only for approved purposes, complete required training, avoid unauthorized disclosure, and report suspected misuse or incidents.
Student-Athlete Representatives
Provide feedback on transparency, education, perceived benefits, and potential unintended impacts of technology use.

6. Levels of review
The level of review depends on three things: what data the technology touches, how many units it serves, and what the department is committing to in cost and contract term.
Level
Applies when
Review includes
Level 1Standard Review
No athlete data; single unit; low or one-time cost
Compliance, Privacy, Ownership, Transparency, Interoperability
Level 2Enhanced Review
Performance data, multi-team use, or recurring cost
Full review
Level 3Comprehensive Review
Physiologic or health data; external data sharing; third-party processing of athlete data
Full review, plus data protection review and Health & Wellness / medical sign-off

The level is proposed by the requester at intake and confirmed at the control points.
7. Exceptions
7.1  Urgent and “emergency” requests
Urgent requests clear the same control points, with a short risk checklist completed at intake to surface issues that would otherwise delay the request: data category, contract term, integration dependency, and whether athlete data leaves Baylor.
A request directed by an administrative lead enters the expedited lane on receipt. This provides documentation for what qualifies as urgent, so the distinction does not have to be determined on a case-by-case basis at intake. An expedited request still clears both control points and still carries the review level its data and commitment call for.
8. The three phases
Phase 1 — Proposal, Approval, Purchase
1.1  A request is initiated by the Director of Applied Performance, a Head Coach, or any Admin Unit Director.
1.2  The requester completes the Technology Idea Form and the internal ATH Form. The request must declare its data category and proposed review level.
1.3  The request goes to the Business Office. The Business Office serves as the filter for all requests and the first control point.
1.4  The forms are submitted to ITS for technical, security, and integration review. This is the second control point.
1.5  The request is evaluated against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard.
1.6  A request is disseminated for purchase only after clearing both control points. Declined requests are returned with documented reasons.
1.7  The Director of Applied Performance holds a weekly standing meeting with the ITS representative to review the status of all open requests across all units. The requester may be brought into the meeting where input is needed; their standing attendance is not expected. The Director of Applied Performance provides regular updates on the status of any open request.
Phase 2 — Implementation and Product Use
2.1  A project manager is assigned. This may be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied, depending on the unit and the system.
2.2  Status flows from the weekly ITS standing meeting through the Director of Applied to the assigned project manager and stakeholders, so that every open request has a known owner.
2.3  Open requests are tracked as follows: project, item, requester, project manager, date submitted, desired implementation date, current status, and what is holding it up.
Phase 3 — Product Review and Renewal Decision
3.1  Review is triggered at six months, or at the end of the competitive season, whichever is longer. Tools used primarily in season are therefore judged on in-season usage.
3.2  The review compares actual utilization against the intent stated on the original request.
3.3  Low utilization opens a diagnostic conversation before a renewal conclusion.
3.4  The outcome is renew, modify or renegotiate, or discontinue.

9. Workflow

input.content:
# Talking Points — INITIAL DISCUSSION: ATH Technology/Software Review

**Meeting:** Thu 2026-08-13, 4:15–4:45 PM Central, MS Teams
**Prepared by:** Eric Rash, Applied Performance
**Companion:** Executive Summary (2pp), already circulated.

**Settled, no longer needs meeting time:** review level naming
(Level 1 Standard / Level 2 Enhanced / Level 3 Comprehensive) is confirmed.

---

# Shareable — safe to paste into email or Teams

Discussion items beyond what the executive summary covers, roughly in order of how
much they need a decision.

**1. Trial and pilot pathway.** The Technology Idea Form asks "Is this a trial or
pilot?" and offers "Provisional / trial" as an approval status, and the Evaluation
Scorecard offers "Approve as trial with hard end date." The framework body does not
currently define a trial: what it is, who tracks the end date, or whether it
re-enters the process to become permanent. Worth deciding whether to add a short
trials section or remove the option from the instruments so the two agree.

**2. Route for zero-cost tools.** The Business Office is the first control point and
filters on budget, contract, and duplication. A free or no-cost application has none
of the three, and Level 1 keys partly on cost. Worth confirming what routes a no-cost
tool into the process, since a free tool touching athlete data is a Level 3 request
with no budget footprint.

**3. Baseline inventory of technology already in use.** The framework establishes a
scheduled renewal decision for requests that come through it. It does not create the
inventory of what the department already owns or when those agreements end. Owner and
timeline for that baseline are not yet assigned.

**4. Student-Athlete Notice.** The term is defined in §2.4 but is not required at any
phase or review level. Given that §3 positions this framework as Baylor's
implementation of NCAA SSI guidance, and that guidance emphasizes athlete
transparency, worth deciding whether notice becomes a required step and at which
level.

**5. Data handling at discontinuation.** Phase 3 can conclude "discontinue," and
Procurement's role requires contracts to address retention, deletion, and
portability. There is no phase step that executes return or deletion of athlete data
when a product is discontinued.

**6. Scope confirmation.** The framework is written to cover all Athletics
technology, with athlete performance technology as the originating context and
highest-risk category. Worth confirming that department-wide scope is what the group
intends.

**7. Effective date and in-flight requests.** No start date is stated, and there is
no transition handling for requests already underway or for purchases made outside
the process.

---
---

# Prep notes — do not send

Filter: every item requires someone else to **agree, decide, or commit a resource**.
Descriptive material is already in the summary and was cut.

## 1. Trials and pilots — a verified inconsistency, and the strongest item

**Verified:** Form 1 (`Form_1_Technology_Idea_Form.docx`) asks "Is this a trial or
pilot?" and lists "☐ Provisional / trial" among approval outcomes. The Scorecard
lists "☐ Approve as trial with hard end date." The framework body contains **zero**
occurrences of trial, pilot, or demo.

**Why the mismatch exists:** all three instruments are dated Aug 4. The §8.2
trials/pilots section was cut from the Aug 11 base. The forms were never revised to
match — a loose end from the merge, not a defect.

**Say:** "The forms and scorecard both offer a trial approval, but the framework
doesn't define one. Do we want a short trials paragraph back, or should the trial
option come off the forms?"

**Why it matters beyond tidiness:** a trial is the most common way technology enters
a department, and it's the case where the cost trigger and the data trigger diverge
hardest — a free 30-day trial reads as low-cost while potentially sending athlete
data to a vendor. If a trial can be approved with a hard end date, someone has to own
that date or the trial quietly becomes permanent.

## 2. Zero-cost tools — the structural version of the same problem

The Business Office is the **first** control point, filtering on "budget, contract,
and duplication." A free app has no budget line, no contract, and often no
duplication signal. Meanwhile Level 1 applies when there is "no athlete data; single
unit; low or one-time cost."

So the entry point least likely to trip the filter is the one that can carry the most
risk: a free tool that touches athlete data. Nothing in Phase 1 routes a no-cost
request differently.

**Say:** "What gets a free tool into the funnel? The Business Office filter is budget
and contract, and a free app has neither."

**What you want:** agreement that data category, not cost, is what triggers intake —
and ideally one sentence added to Phase 1 saying so.

## 3. Baseline inventory — carried forward, still unassigned

§4 promises "a consistent, shared understanding of the entire inventory of software
and technology in use across the department." Phase 3 reviews utilization "against
the intent stated on the original request." Those only connect for technology that
came in through the framework. Anything bought earlier has no originating request, no
owner, and no renewal date on a calendar.

**Say:** "The renewal gate works going forward. It doesn't tell us what we're already
paying for or when those agreements end. Who owns building that baseline, and by
when?"

## 4. Student-Athlete Notice — defined but never required

"Student-Athlete Notice" is defined in §2.4 as a plain-language explanation to
athletes of what data is collected, why, who can access it, retention, and rights.
That definition is the **only** appearance in the framework — no phase step, no role,
and no review level requires one to exist.

**Guard against a false correction:** Form 2 contains the word "notice," but it reads
"Notice period to cancel" — contract cancellation, a different concept. Form 2 does
ask "Consent considerations flagged?", but nothing in the process says who resolves a
flag. So the gap is real; don't let the form's wording talk you out of it.

Related: "Student-Athlete Representatives" is a listed role in §5 providing feedback
on transparency, with no mechanism connecting them to any actual request.

**Why it lands:** §3 states this framework *is* Baylor's implementation of NCAA SSI
guidance, and athlete transparency is central to that guidance. This is the gap most
likely to be flagged when the document reaches OGC and Privacy — better to raise it
yourself now.

## 5. Discontinuation doesn't close the data loop

Phase 3.4 outcomes are "renew, modify or renegotiate, or discontinue." Procurement's
role in §5 requires vendor contracts to address "retention, deletion, portability."
But no phase step triggers return or deletion of athlete data when something is
discontinued. Zero occurrences of exit, termination, or offboarding in the framework.

The contract language exists; nothing invokes it. This is the second item OGC/Privacy
will find.

## 6. Scope — the sentences to point at if pressed

- **§1.2** — "The process below applies to every technology request in the
  department, and the depth of review depends on the request's scope."
- **§2.1** — "The framework is not limited to performance, health, and wellness…
  A request that does not involve any athlete data still goes through the same
  review mechanism."

The phrase "department-wide" no longer appears in §2.1 after the last edit pass; the
idea is fully carried by those two sentences. If someone wants the words back, that's
a one-line change.

## 7. Effective date, in-flight requests, and bypass detection

Three absences with one root — the framework has no occurrences of effective date,
transition, enforcement, violation, or non-compliance:

- No stated start date.
- No handling for requests already underway when this takes effect.
- The Athletics Executive Sponsor "ensures teams, coaches, and staff use approved
  technologies," but nothing states how an off-process purchase is detected or what
  follows. Tie this to item 2 — if it never touches the budget, nothing catches it.

Lowest priority of the seven for a 30-minute initial discussion, but the first
question a skeptical reader asks is "when does this start."

## If it comes up

- **The framework commits other departments' time.** Two control points in fixed
  order, nothing purchased until both clear, ITS represented at a supervisory level
  with authority to commit ITS resources, plus a weekly standing meeting. The
  substantive change worth naming: this moves "who can say no" into a documented
  order. Keep the framing on what the *request* demands, never on staffing.

- **Level declaration is self-proposed.** §6 says the level "is proposed by the
  requester at intake and confirmed at the control points." Confirming it depends on
  knowing what data the technology touches, which at intake is the vendor's claim.
  Fine as designed, but if someone probes the weak point, this is it.

- **Does this become policy?** Currently an Athletics-specific overlay routing into
  existing Baylor governance rather than around it (§2.3). Whether it needs an
  OGC/University policy path is a real question — first thing to drop for time.

- **Urgency gate — already documented.** A request directed by an administrative lead
  enters the expedited lane on receipt and still clears both control points, and
  still carries the review level its data calls for.

## Questions to leave with

1. Trials: restore a framework section, or strip the option from the forms?
2. Who owns the baseline inventory of technology already in use, and by when?
3. Does Student-Athlete Notice become a required step, and at which level?

"Student-Athlete Notice" is defined in §2.4 as a plain-language explanation to
athletes of what data is collected, why, who can access it, retention, and rights.
That definition is the **only** appearance in the framework — no phase step, no role,
and no review level requires one to exist.

**Guard against a false correction:** Form 2 contains the word "notice," but it reads
"Notice period to cancel" — contract cancellation, a different concept. Form 2 does
ask "Consent considerations flagged?", but nothing in the process says who resolves a
flag. So the gap is real; don't let the form's wording talk you out of it.

Related: "Student-Athlete Representatives" is a listed role in §5 providing feedback
on transparency, with no mechanism connecting them to any actual request.

**Why it lands:** §3 states this framework *is* Baylor's implementation of NCAA SSI
guidance, and athlete transparency is central to that guidance. This is the gap most
likely to be flagged when the document reaches OGC and Privacy — better to raise it
yourself now.

## 5. Discontinuation doesn't close the data loop

Phase 3.4 outcomes are "renew, modify or renegotiate, or discontinue." Procurement's
role in §5 requires vendor contracts to address "retention, deletion, portability."
But no phase step triggers return or deletion of athlete data when something is
discontinued. Zero occurrences of exit, termination, or offboarding in the framework.

The contract language exists; nothing invokes it. This is the second item OGC/Privacy
will find.

## 6. Scope — the sentences to point at if pressed

- **§1.2** — "The process below applies to every technology request in the
  department, and the depth of review depends on the request's scope."
- **§2.1** — "The framework is not limited to performance, health, and wellness…

  review mechanism."

idea is fully carried by those two sentences. If someone wants the words back, that's
a one-line change.

## 7. Effective date, in-flight requests, and bypass detection

Three absences with one root — the framework has no occurrences of effective date,
transition, enforcement, violation, or non-compliance:

- No stated start date.
- No handling for requests already underway when this takes effect.
- The Athletics Executive Sponsor "ensures teams, coaches, and staff use approved
  technologies," but nothing states how an off-process purchase is detected or what
  follows. Tie this to item 2 — if it never touches the budget, nothing catches it.

question a skeptical reader asks is "when does this start."

  order, nothing purchased until both clear, ITS represented at a supervisory level
  with authority to commit ITS resources, plus a weekly standing meeting. The
  substantive change worth naming: this moves "who can say no" into a documented
  order. Keep the framing on what the *request* demands, never on staffing.

  knowing what data the technology touches, which at intake is the vendor's claim.

3. Does Student-Athlete Notice become a required step, and at which level?

content.content:
Fireflies CLI — Every Fireflies meeting feature, plus offline search, cross-meeting intelligence, and a local database no other tool ha…

Highlights (not in the official API docs):
  • transcripts search   Full-text search across all synced meeting transcripts without consuming any API quota.
  • person timeline   Chronological meeting history with a specific person — topics, action items, and talk ratio per meeting.
  • action-items list   Aggregate action items from all meetings in a date range — weekly commitment audit in one command.
  • transcripts find   Find meetings by participant email, channel name, keyword, or date range — all client-side, no broken API date filters.
  • transcripts status   Show PROCESSED / PROCESSING / FAILED status for recent meetings upfront — know before you fetch.
  • topics list   Most frequent topics across all meetings in a date range — what is actually consuming meeting time.
  • digest   Aggregate view of all recent meetings: titles, gists, topics, and action items in one structured output.
  • transcripts export   Export a transcript as markdown to a vault directory with auto-generated YYYY-MM-DD_title.md filename.

Agent mode: add --agent to any command for JSON output + non-interactive mode.
Health check: run 'fireflies-pp-cli doctor' to verify auth and connectivity.
See README.md or the bundled SKILL.md for recipes.

Usage:
  fireflies-pp-cli [command]

Available Commands:
  action-items  Extract action items from transcripts
  agent-context Emit structured JSON describing this CLI for agents
  analytics     Query meeting analytics
  api           Browse all API endpoints by interface name
  auth          Manage authentication for Fireflies
  channels      Get a single channel
  completion    Generate the autocompletion script for the specified shell
  digest        Aggregate summary of recent meetings — titles, decisions, and action items
  doctor        Check CLI health
  feedback      Record feedback about this CLI (local by default; upstream opt-in)
  help          Help about any command
  import        Import data from JSONL file via API create/upsert calls
  keywords      Get AI-extracted keywords for a transcript
  person        Person-centric views across all meetings
  profile       Named sets of flags saved for reuse
  speakers      Show per-speaker analytics for a transcript
  summary       Get the AI-generated summary for a transcript
  sync          Sync Fireflies transcripts to local SQLite for offline search and analysis
  topics        Extract and analyze topics from transcripts
  transcripts   List, search, and manage meeting transcripts
  users         Get a single user
  version       Print version
  which         Find the command that implements a capability
  workflow      Compound workflows that combine multiple API operations

Flags:
      --agent                Set all agent-friendly defaults (--json --compact --no-input --no-color --yes)
      --compact              Return only key fields (id, name, status, timestamps) for minimal token usage
      --config string        Config file path
      --csv                  Output as CSV (table and array responses)

# Meeting Record — Data / Technology / Software Proposal

**Date:** 2026-08-13, 4:16 PM Central · 39.5 min · MS Teams
**Source:** Fireflies transcript `01KZYFQ9F92NHG57AHSQJ2DFR4` (476 sentences, full text reviewed)
**Speakers:** Kenny Boyd (chair), Micah Lamb (ITS), Jon Allen (ITS), Lisa Creed,
Erin Boyette (Business Office), Cody Hall (Athletics Business Office),
Jovon Overshown (Athletics)

> Note: the auto-summary names "Aaron" and "Carrie." The actual speaker is **Erin
> Boyette**; **Carrie** is referenced but did not speak. Eric does not appear in the
> speaker list and is referred to in the third person ("Coach Rasch").

---

## Headline outcome

**Micah Lamb is writing a counter-proposal and sending it to the same group.**

His position, stated directly: the problems are real and the content is good, but he
does not want a **parallel** framework or flow.

> "I really don't think we need to go that far to solve a lot of the problems that
> we're seeing today. If we instead had a more standardized intake and a more
> standardized framework around the requests coming from athletics, that would really
> streamline and speed up the path through the existing process… That's where I think
> we will see most of our gain for less effort."

He was complimentary throughout — "I really like it," "I like where it's coming
from," "it's not a lot, man" — so this reads as a scoping disagreement, not a
rejection. The question he is answering is *how much new process is warranted*, and
his answer is: less than the framework proposes.

**The convergence point was a one-page checklist.** Kenny: "the more simple and
concise, almost like one page checklist." Lisa agreed immediately. Micah described
the same thing as a worksheet telling requesters what they'll need before review,
including what to get from the vendor early, while the vendor is still selling.

## What validated the framework

Four things in the document were independently named as the fix:

1. **Declaring the data category up front.** Micah's strongest endorsement — this is
   the single biggest source of delay today. "That piece alone will shave weeks off
   the process… that has always been what's taken us the longest." Different people
   call the same data different things; a common language resolves it.
2. **Standardized intake.** "The one thing I saw that I really liked in the proposal
   is standardizing that intake from an athletics perspective." He confirmed ITS
   already does exactly this for other divisions with diverse needs, including a
   priority-ordering step before the request hits the ITS workflow.
3. **Business Office as the first control point.** Kenny described the design and
   Micah confirmed it matches how deans operate — requests go to the business officer
   first for a funding go/no-go that is "not necessarily a decision at that point."
4. **The inventory problem.** Jon Allen: "nobody knows everything that exists."
   80–90% of platforms are known; the remainder surface as surprises years later.
   Kenny closed with "I do think we need to figure out all the systems that we're
   using." This was the meeting's opening theme and its closing one.

## The main risk raised

**Jon Allen's serial-process warning.** Review times have improved substantially, and
he wants to avoid two sequential processes turning a two-week turnaround into eight to
ten weeks. Micah echoed it as "how do we interleave these so it doesn't feel like I'm
doing the same thing two times." Any defense of the framework has to answer this.

Context that makes it concrete: ~1,000 IDEA form requests came through last year,
roughly three a day, arriving in clumps rather than evenly.

## New problems surfaced that the framework does not currently address

- **Multiple entry points are the actual bottleneck.** Micah listed them: email from
  a coach, email from procurement via TCM, IDEA form submission, business office,
  strength and conditioning. Each carries different information. Cody and Kenny put
  it at roughly 80% coming through the right channel and **20% bypassing** — and that
  20% causes disproportionate delay and administrative burden.

- **TCM/IDEA form chicken-and-egg — this one directly contradicts "Business Office
  first."** Erin Boyette explained that a staff member can complete the **entire** IT
  review before the business office ever sees the request, because the business office
  only encounters it at the contract stage, where a TCM submission requires an IT
  project ID. Procurement added that ID requirement to the TCM form without ITS
  knowing. So the university's own mechanics can route around the first control point.

- **Discovery before product selection.** Jon Allen cautioned against people arriving
  at the business office with a product already chosen. Better: "I have this
  challenge" → check whether an existing solution already meets it. The framework has
  no needs-discovery step ahead of intake; it begins with a request for a named product.

- **Cross-domain sign-off is genuinely unresolved.** Micah: "when it crosses those
  domains, is there an expectation that every domain signs off in athletics?" Not
  knowing who to call is a documented cause of delay. This is what §5 Roles is for,
  but the routing is not explicit.

- **Simple vs. complex needs defined parameters.** Lisa: if you create two paths you
  "would have to define what that means… what the parameters are." §6 already does
  this — Level 1/2/3 with stated triggers. Worth pointing at directly, since the room
  asked for something the document already contains.

## Commitments made

| Who | What |
|---|---|
| Micah | Write the counter-proposal and send to the same group |
| Micah | Add Athletics Business Office to IDEA form auto-notifications — can start for athletics immediately pending Cody's OK |
| Micah | Add a business-officer dropdown to the IDEA form; campus-wide default by mid-fall |
| Micah | Offered to auto-loop Kenny's team on any athletics request involving athlete data |
| Kenny | Internal debrief with Cody and Jovon on the athletics position |
| Kenny | Separate session with Micah, Erin, possibly Carrie on HIPAA email/inbox challenges |
| — | Nothing currently in the pipeline is held up pending a new process |

## Unresolved / friction

- **HIPAA mailbox request.** Erin says it was a group email mischaracterized as HIPAA
  intake; Micah says the email explicitly stated HIPAA intake. Deferred to a separate
  conversation. Jon Allen confirmed there is **no HIPAA-compliant email solution**
  today — the closest is an email-enabled Box folder that cannot send.

- **Kenny's closing frustration.** Nine years of the same answer that athletics
  systems don't connect with campus health and counseling. He acknowledged the
  campus EMR investment but said plainly it doesn't solve athletics' problem. Worth
  knowing the temperature going into any follow-up.

## Implications for the framework document

1. The likely landing zone is **not** the full three-phase framework as a standalone
   process. It is the framework's *content* — data category declaration, review
   levels, standardized intake — delivered as a one-page instrument that feeds the
   existing university workflow.
2. That reframing preserves the parts the room endorsed and drops the part it
   resisted (a parallel process). Worth deciding whether to get ahead of Micah's
   counter-proposal with this, or wait and respond to it.
3. The trials/pilots inconsistency, Student-Athlete Notice gap, and discontinuation
   data loop identified pre-meeting were **not** discussed and remain open.
4. Add: needs-discovery before product selection, and a route that survives the
   TCM/IDEA-form ordering problem.
