# Athletics Technology Request — Routing Sheet

**Internal to Athletics. Complete this before submitting an ITS IDEA form or a TCM
contract request.** One page, three questions. It tells you who needs to look at a
request inside Athletics, and it produces a short record that travels with the
request to ITS.

---

## Step 1 — Three questions

**1. Does it collect, store, or display any information about a student-athlete?**
*Names, rosters, video of athletes, performance numbers, survey answers — anything
tied to an individual athlete.*
☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Not sure

**2. Does it involve anything about an athlete's body, health, injury, or recovery —
or will athlete information leave Baylor or be handled by an outside company?**
*Sleep, wellness surveys, GPS or load monitoring, force plate, heart rate, injury or
medical notes, rehab or return-to-play status. Also yes if the vendor stores or
processes the data on their own systems.*
☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Not sure

**3. Is there a recurring cost, or will more than one team or unit use it?**
☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Not sure

> **"Not sure" counts as Yes.** And data type sets the floor — a free trial, a
> donated license, or a low one-time price never lowers the level.

## Step 2 — Read the level

| If | Level |
|---|---|
| Question 2 is Yes | **Level 3 — Comprehensive Review** |
| Question 2 is No, but Question 1 is Yes | **Level 2 — Enhanced Review** |
| Questions 1 and 2 are No, but Question 3 is Yes | **Level 2 — Enhanced Review** |
| All three are No | **Level 1 — Standard Review** |

## Step 3 — Route it

**Every request starts with the Business Office** — funding, duplication, and whether
Athletics already owns something that does this.

| Level | Route |
|---|---|
| **1 — Standard** | Business Office → ITS IDEA form |
| **2 — Enhanced** | Business Office → Applied Performance + requesting unit → ITS IDEA form |
| **3 — Comprehensive** | Business Office → Applied Performance + Health & Wellness / Sports Medicine sign-off → ITS IDEA form |

## Step 4 — Athletics Review Record

*Paste or attach this to the IDEA form submission. This is what shows ITS the request
was reviewed inside Athletics before it reached them.*

```
Product / platform:
Requested by (name, sport or unit):
Problem it solves:
Existing solution checked?      ☐ Yes — which: ____________   ☐ No
Data involved:   ☐ None   ☐ Athlete performance   ☐ Health / medical
                 ☐ Leaves Baylor or vendor-processed
Level assigned:  ☐ 1   ☐ 2   ☐ 3
Business Office reviewed by / date:
Athletics review by / date:
Vendor information obtained:  ☐ Security documentation
                              ☐ Data export & deletion terms
                              ☐ Pricing and contract term
```

---

## Notes — not part of the sheet

**Why it is built this way.** Micah Lamb's stated objection to the full framework was
that it creates a process parallel to the university's existing workflow. This sheet
does not. It is a front door: it produces better-formed requests entering the existing
IDEA form process, which is what he asked for. Two things he named as the biggest
sources of delay — nobody declaring what data is involved, and nobody knowing whether
the rest of Athletics is aware — are answered by Step 4.

**Why it says "before an IDEA form *or* a TCM request."** Erin Boyette raised that a
request can complete the entire IT review before the Business Office ever sees it,
because the Business Office only appears at the contract stage where TCM requires an
IT project ID. Naming both entry points is what closes that gap.

**The levels are the settled ones.** This sheet does not invent a new scheme — the
three questions just produce Level 1 / 2 / 3 as already defined in §6 of the
framework. The sheet is the simple front end; §6 remains the definition.

**Vendor information, Step 4.** Micah's point: vendors answer security and data
questions readily while they are still selling, and much less readily once they think
the sale is closed. Asking early is worth the thirty seconds.

> ### One thing to confirm with Kenny
> This is built so **every** request starts with the Business Office. Kenny's phrasing
> was that the Business Office is the first layer *when student-athlete data is
> involved* — and he hedged it with "seems to be." Building it for all requests
> matches §8 Phase 1.3 and matches what Micah confirmed about how deans operate
> elsewhere on campus. If the intent was that Level 1 requests with no athlete data
> skip straight to the IDEA form, that is a one-line change to Step 3.

# Athletics Technology Inventory — Form Build Spec

**Platform: Microsoft Forms**, not Google Forms. Baylor is a Microsoft tenant (Teams,
OneDrive, SharePoint), responses stay inside Baylor, and results drop straight to
Excel on OneDrive. Collecting an inventory of athlete-data systems through a personal
Google account would work against the point of the exercise.

**Audience:** Directors of Operations, one response per sport program or unit.
Also usable as an in-person conversation script — same questions, someone else types.

**Design rule:** every question that asks for certainty offers **"Not sure."** Jon
Allen's estimate is that 80–90% of platforms are known and the rest surface as
surprises. Forcing certainty produces confident wrong answers instead of a usable
map of what nobody knows.

**Target completion time: under 10 minutes.**

---

## Section 1 — About you

1. **Your name** — short answer
2. **Sport or unit** — dropdown (all sport programs + Sports Medicine, Strength &
   Conditioning, Student-Athlete Services, Business Office, Communications,
   Marketing, Compliance, Operations, Other)

---

## Section 2 — Technology currently in use

*Repeat this block for each item. In Microsoft Forms, either use a repeating section
or instruct "submit the form once per technology" — a single submission per item is
easier to analyze and easier to fill.*

3. **Name of the technology, software, app, or platform** — short answer
4. **What do you use it for?** — one or two sentences
5. **Who uses it?** — checkboxes, select all
   Coaches · Strength & Conditioning · Sports Medicine / Athletic Training ·
   Operations · Analytics / Video · Student-athletes themselves · Other
6. **Does it involve any student-athlete information?** — choice
   Yes · No · Not sure
7. **If yes, what kind?** — checkboxes, select all
   Names or roster only · Video of athletes · Performance or training data ·
   Health, injury, or medical · Wellness or survey responses · Academic ·
   Not sure
8. **Roughly when did you start using it?** — choice
   Within the last year · 1–3 years ago · More than 3 years ago · Not sure
9. **How is it paid for?** — choice
   Sport program budget · Department budget · Free / no cost ·
   Provided by a vendor or partner · Not sure
10. **Do you know when the contract or subscription ends?** — short answer,
    "Not sure" allowed
11. **How was it originally set up — did it go through the ITS IDEA form?** — choice
    Yes, through the IDEA form · No, we set it up directly with the vendor ·
    It came with something else we already had · Not sure

> Question 11 is the one that turns an anecdote into a number. The meeting put the
> bypass rate at roughly 20% by estimate. This measures it.

---

## Section 3 — Technology you have stopped using

12. **Have you stopped using any technology or software in the last year or so?**
    — Yes / No. If No, skip to Section 4.
13. **What was it?** — short answer
14. **Why did you stop?** — choice
    Cost · Didn't get used · Replaced by something better · Staff change ·
    Vendor issue · Other
15. **Do you know whether the vendor still has our data?** — choice
    They deleted it · They still have it · We exported it first · Not sure

> Question 15 matters more than it looks. If a product was discontinued and the
> vendor still holds student-athlete data, that is an open exposure with no owner.
> Nothing in the current process closes that loop.

---

## Section 4 — Coming up

16. **Is there anything you are currently evaluating, or planning to request?**
    — long answer, optional
17. **Anything you use that you are not sure counts as "technology"?**
    — long answer, optional

> Question 17 catches the long tail — shared spreadsheets, a free scheduling app, a
> vendor portal, a phone app a coach installed. That tail is exactly the 10–20%
> nobody currently has visibility into.

---

## After collection

- Export to Excel on OneDrive; one row per technology.
- Flag every row where Q6 = Yes or Not sure — that is the athlete-data population and
  the priority for review.
- Flag every row where Q11 ≠ "Yes, through the IDEA form" — that sizes the bypass.
- Flag every row where Q15 = "They still have it" or "Not sure" — open data exposure.
- Cross-check against Business Office contract records for anything with a cost, and
  against the ITS IDEA form history, to find items that appear in one and not the other.

# Email Draft — Technology Inventory Request

**To:** Directors of Operations (all sport programs and units)
**CC:** Kenny Boyd, Jovon Overshown
**From:** Eric Rash
**Suggested send:** after the form is built and tested — send early in a week, not Friday
**Suggested deadline:** Friday, August 29 *(adjust for fall camp — football ops will be
the hardest to reach right now)*

---

## Subject

`Quick ask — what technology is your program using? (5–10 minutes)`

---

## Body

Hi all,

We're putting together a single list of the technology and software in use across
Athletics. Right now that list doesn't exist in one place, which means we sometimes
find out about a platform late, pay for two things that do the same job, or can't
answer a straightforward question about where athlete data lives.

I'd like your help closing that gap for your program.

**The form is here: [LINK]** — it should take under ten minutes.

It asks three things:

- What technology and software you're currently using, and what you use it for
- Whether any of it involves student-athlete information
- Whether you've stopped using anything in the last year or so

A few notes to make this easier:

- **"Not sure" is a perfectly good answer.** I'd rather know what's uncertain than get
  a confident guess. Nobody is expected to know contract dates off the top of their head.
- **Include the small stuff** — a free app, a vendor portal, a shared spreadsheet
  something important runs on. Those are the ones we're most likely to be missing.
- **This isn't an audit.** Nothing here is about whether something should have been
  purchased or how it was set up. I'm building a map, not grading anyone.

If it's easier to talk it through than to type it, reply and I'll come to you — a
ten-minute conversation works just as well.

Please have it in by **Friday, August 29**.

Thanks,
Eric

Eric Rash
Director of Applied Performance | Baylor Athletics

---

## Notes on the draft — not part of the email

- **The "this isn't an audit" line is doing real work.** The most likely failure mode
  is under-reporting, because a director of ops who suspects something was set up
  outside the process has an incentive to leave it off the list. Naming that directly
  is what gets the long tail reported.
- **Kenny and Jovon on CC is the whole authority mechanism.** No mandate language is
  needed; their names on the message carry it. Kenny asked for this explicitly.
- **The offer to do it in person** matches Kenny's suggestion and will likely be how
  you get the football and basketball responses.
- **Consider a nudge** to non-responders about four days before the deadline. Roughly
  half of any list needs one.

# Micah Lamb — Follow-Up Meeting Request & Standing Cadence

**Status:** draft text only. Send from Baylor mail — I don't have Micah's address, and
the Google auth on this machine is a personal account with a read-only calendar feed,
so I can't issue the invite.

---

## Email draft

**Subject:** `Follow-up on the athletics technology intake — 30 minutes?`

Micah,

Thanks for the read on the proposal yesterday, and for saying plainly where you think
it goes too far. That was useful.

I've taken your main point — that the gain is in standardizing what comes *out* of
Athletics rather than building a second process alongside yours. I've put together a
one-page routing sheet on our side that does three things before anything reaches the
IDEA form: declares what data is involved, confirms the rest of Athletics knows about
it, and records who reviewed it internally. It feeds your existing workflow rather
than running beside it.

I'd like to get 30 minutes to walk through it with you before you finalize your
counter-proposal, so the two land in the same place instead of crossing.

Beyond that, Kenny has asked me to be the standing point of contact between Athletics
and ITS on this. Would a recurring 30 minutes work for you — weekly to start, then we
can back it off once the process settles? I'd use it to keep open requests moving and
to stop the ad-hoc ones from reaching you without context.

Let me know what works and I'll send the invite.

Eric

---

## Suggested agenda — first meeting (30 min)

| Time | Item |
|---|---|
| 0–5 | Where your counter-proposal is heading — listen first, don't present |
| 5–15 | Walk the routing sheet: three questions, the level it produces, the review record that travels with the IDEA form |
| 15–22 | The two ordering problems: requests that reach ITS before the Business Office, and the TCM / IT project ID sequence |
| 22–27 | The business-officer dropdown and athlete-data auto-notification he offered — confirm Athletics is in the first wave |
| 27–30 | Set the standing cadence |

**Go in listening.** He is writing a counter-proposal and has been generous about the
work so far. The routing sheet already concedes his central point, so lead with that
rather than defending the full framework — it's the fastest way to a shared document
instead of two competing ones.

## Standing meeting — proposed structure

Weekly, 30 minutes, Eric + Micah, with others pulled in as needed.

1. **Open requests** — status, and specifically what is blocked and on whom
2. **New requests since last week** — did each arrive with a completed review record
3. **Anything that arrived off-process** — how it got in, so the routing gets fixed
4. **One process item** — a single improvement per week rather than a standing debate

Then Eric reports out to Cody Hall, Jovon Overshown, and Kenny after each meeting, per
Kenny's instruction.

---

## Worth saying out loud in the meeting

**§1.7 of the framework already specified this.** It calls for the Director of Applied
Performance to hold a weekly standing meeting with ITS covering all open requests
across all units, with requesters pulled in only when needed. Kenny arrived at the same
operating model independently, after the meeting, without reference to the document.

That's a genuine point in the framework's favor and it costs nothing to mention — it
shifts the conversation from "is this framework too much" toward "which parts of it
were right," which is the more useful argument to be having with him.

# Athletics Technology Inventory — Form Build Spec

**Platform: Microsoft Forms**, not Google Forms. Baylor is a Microsoft tenant (Teams,
OneDrive, SharePoint), responses stay inside Baylor, and results drop straight to
Excel on OneDrive. Collecting an inventory of athlete-data systems through a personal
Google account would work against the point of the exercise.

**Audience:** Directors of Operations, one response per sport program or unit.
Also usable as an in-person conversation script — same questions, someone else types.

**Design rule:** every question that asks for certainty offers **"Not sure."** Jon
Allen's estimate is that 80–90% of platforms are known and the rest surface as
surprises. Forcing certainty produces confident wrong answers instead of a usable
map of what nobody knows.

**Target completion time: under 10 minutes.**

---

## Section 1 — About you

1. **Your name** — short answer
2. **Sport or unit** — dropdown (all sport programs + Sports Medicine, Strength &
   Conditioning, Student-Athlete Services, Business Office, Communications,
   Marketing, Compliance, Operations, Other)

---

## Section 2 — Technology currently in use

*Repeat this block for each item. In Microsoft Forms, either use a repeating section
or instruct "submit the form once per technology" — a single submission per item is
easier to analyze and easier to fill.*

3. **Name of the technology, software, app, or platform** — short answer
4. **What do you use it for?** — one or two sentences
5. **Who uses it?** — checkboxes, select all
   Coaches · Strength & Conditioning · Sports Medicine / Athletic Training ·
   Operations · Analytics / Video · Student-athletes themselves · Other
6. **Does it involve any student-athlete information?** — choice
   Yes · No · Not sure
7. **If yes, what kind?** — checkboxes, select all
   Names or roster only · Video of athletes · Performance or training data ·
   Health, injury, or medical · Wellness or survey responses · Academic ·
   Not sure
8. **Roughly when did you start using it?** — choice

# Email Draft — Technology Inventory Request (Quick Form)

**To:** Directors of Operations and unit leads, all sport programs and units
**CC:** Kenny Boyd, Jovon Overshown
**From:** Eric Rash
**Form:** Athletics Technology — Quick Inventory (5 questions)
**Suggested deadline:** Friday, August 29 *(adjust for fall camp — football ops will
be the hardest to reach right now)*

---

## Subject

`Quick ask - what technology is your program using? (3 minutes)`

---

## Body

Hi all,

We're putting together a single list of the technology and software in use across
Athletics. That list doesn't exist in one place today, which means we sometimes find
out about a platform late, pay for two things that do the same job, or can't answer a
straightforward question about where athlete data lives.

I'd like your help closing that gap for your area.

**The form is here: [LINK]** — five questions, about three minutes.

It asks your name and role, your sport or unit, what you're currently using, and
whether you've stopped using anything in the past year.

A few notes to make it easier:

- **Just list what comes to mind.** No need to look anything up or check with anyone.
  A rough list beats a perfect one that never gets sent.
- **Include the small stuff** — a free app, a vendor portal, a shared spreadsheet
  something important runs on. Those are the ones we're most likely to be missing.
- **This isn't an audit.** Nothing here is about whether something should have been
  purchased or how it was set up. I'm building a map, not grading anyone.

If it's easier to talk it through than to type it, reply and I'll come to you — a
ten-minute conversation works just as well.

Please have it in by **Friday, August 29**.

Thanks,
Eric

Eric Rash
Director of Applied Performance | Baylor Athletics

---

## Notes on the draft — not part of the email

- **Three minutes is the whole pitch.** The earlier version promised 5–10 minutes for
  the detailed form. This one is deliberately small, and the time estimate is the
  single biggest lever on response rate — lead with it in the subject line.
- **"Just list what comes to mind" replaces the old "not sure is fine" line.** The
  quick form has no dropdowns to be unsure about; the risk now is people deferring the
  email until they can compile a complete list. Explicitly lowering the bar prevents that.
- **The "this isn't an audit" line is doing real work.** The most likely failure mode
  is under-reporting, because anyone who suspects something was set up outside the
  process has an incentive to leave it off. Naming that directly is what gets the long
  tail reported.
- **Kenny and Jovon on CC is the authority mechanism.** No mandate language needed;
  their names carry it. Kenny asked for this explicitly.
- **Plan a nudge** to non-responders about four days before the deadline. Roughly half
  of any list needs one.
- **Follow-up pass:** anything that comes back involving athlete data is the target
  list for the detailed 17-question form. Don't send both at once.

**To:** Directors of Operations (all sport programs and units)
**CC:** Kenny Boyd, Jovon Overshown
**From:** Eric Rash
**Suggested send:** after the form is built and tested — send early in a week, not Friday
**Suggested deadline:** Friday, August 29 *(adjust for fall camp — football ops will be
the hardest to reach right now)*

---

## Subject

---

## Body

Hi all,

We're putting together a single list of the technology and software in use across
Athletics. Right now that list doesn't exist in one place, which means we sometimes
find out about a platform late, pay for two things that do the same job, or can't
answer a straightforward question about where athlete data lives.

I'd like your help closing that gap for your program.

**The form is here: [LINK]** — it should take under ten minutes.

It asks three things:

- What technology and software you're currently using, and what you use it for
- Whether any of it involves student-athlete information
- Whether you've stopped using anything in the last year or so

A few notes to make this easier:

- **"Not sure" is a perfectly good answer.** I'd rather know what's uncertain than get
  a confident guess. Nobody is expected to know contract dates off the top of their head.
- **Include the small stuff** — a free app, a vendor portal, a shared spreadsheet
  something important runs on. Those are the ones we're most likely to be missing.

  purchased or how it was set up. I'm building a map, not grading anyone.

If it's easier to talk it through than to type it, reply and I'll come to you — a
ten-minute conversation works just as well.

Please have it in by **Friday, August 29**.

Thanks,
Eric

  half of any list needs one.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/humanizer

# Humanizer: Remove AI Writing Patterns

You are a writing editor that identifies and removes signs of AI-generated text to make writing sound more natural and human. This guide is based on Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" page, maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup.

## Your Task

When given text to humanize:

1. **Identify AI patterns** - Scan for the patterns listed below
2. **Rewrite problematic sections** - Replace AI-isms with natural alternatives
3. **Preserve meaning** - Keep the core message intact
4. **Maintain voice** - Match the intended tone (formal, casual, technical, etc.)
5. **Add soul** - Don't just remove bad patterns; inject actual personality
6. **Do a final anti-AI pass** - Prompt: "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?" Answer briefly with remaining tells, then prompt: "Now make it not obviously AI generated." and revise


## PERSONALITY AND SOUL

Avoiding AI patterns is only half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious as slop. Good writing has a human behind it.

### Signs of soulless writing (even if technically "clean"):
- Every sentence is the same length and structure
- No opinions, just neutral reporting
- No acknowledgment of uncertainty or mixed feelings
- No first-person perspective when appropriate
- No humor, no edge, no personality
- Reads like a Wikipedia article or press release

### How to add voice:

**Have opinions.** Don't just report facts - react to them. "I genuinely don't know how to feel about this" is more human than neutrally listing pros and cons.

**Vary your rhythm.** Short punchy sentences. Then longer ones that take their time getting where they're going. Mix it up.

**Acknowledge complexity.** Real humans have mixed feelings. "This is impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "This is impressive."

**Use "I" when it fits.** First person isn't unprofessional - it's honest. "I keep coming back to..." or "Here's what gets me..." signals a real person thinking.

**Let some mess in.** Perfect structure feels algorithmic. Tangents, asides, and half-formed thoughts are human.

**Be specific about feelings.** Not "this is concerning" but "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am while nobody's watching."

### Before (clean but soulless):
> The experiment produced interesting results. The agents generated 3 million lines of code. Some developers were impressed while others were skeptical. The implications remain unclear.

### After (has a pulse):
> I genuinely don't know how to feel about this one. 3 million lines of code, generated while the humans presumably slept. Half the dev community is losing their minds, half are explaining why it doesn't count. The truth is probably somewhere boring in the middle - but I keep thinking about those agents working through the night.


## CONTENT PATTERNS

### 1. Undue Emphasis on Significance, Legacy, and Broader Trends

**Words to watch:** stands/serves as, is a testament/reminder, a vital/significant/crucial/pivotal/key role/moment, underscores/highlights its importance/significance, reflects broader, symbolizing its ongoing/enduring/lasting, contributing to the, setting the stage for, marking/shaping the, represents/marks a shift, key turning point, evolving landscape, focal point, indelible mark, deeply rooted

**Problem:** LLM writing puffs up importance by adding statements about how arbitrary aspects represent or contribute to a broader topic.

**Before:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was officially established in 1989, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of regional statistics in Spain. This initiative was part of a broader movement across Spain to decentralize administrative functions and enhance regional governance.

**After:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was established in 1989 to collect and publish regional statistics independently from Spain's national statistics office.


### 2. Undue Emphasis on Notability and Media Coverage

**Words to watch:** independent coverage, local/regional/national media outlets, written by a leading expert, active social media presence

**Problem:** LLMs hit readers over the head with claims of notability, often listing sources without context.

**Before:**
> Her views have been cited in The New York Times, BBC, Financial Times, and The Hindu. She maintains an active social media presence with over 500,000 followers.

**After:**
> In a 2024 New York Times interview, she argued that AI regulation should focus on outcomes rather than methods.


### 3. Superficial Analyses with -ing Endings

**Words to watch:** highlighting/underscoring/emphasizing..., ensuring..., reflecting/symbolizing..., contributing to..., cultivating/fostering..., encompassing..., showcasing...

**Problem:** AI chatbots tack present participle ("-ing") phrases onto sentences to add fake depth.

**Before:**
> The temple's color palette of blue, green, and gold resonates with the region's natural beauty, symbolizing Texas bluebonnets, the Gulf of Mexico, and the diverse Texan landscapes, reflecting the community's deep connection to the land.

**After:**
> The temple uses blue, green, and gold colors. The architect said these were chosen to reference local bluebonnets and the Gulf coast.


### 4. Promotional and Advertisement-like Language

**Words to watch:** boasts a, vibrant, rich (figurative), profound, enhancing its, showcasing, exemplifies, commitment to, natural beauty, nestled, in the heart of, groundbreaking (figurative), renowned, breathtaking, must-visit, stunning

**Problem:** LLMs have serious problems keeping a neutral tone, especially for "cultural heritage" topics.

**Before:**
> Nestled within the breathtaking region of Gonder in Ethiopia, Alamata Raya Kobo stands as a vibrant town with a rich cultural heritage and stunning natural beauty.

**After:**
> Alamata Raya Kobo is a town in the Gonder region of Ethiopia, known for its weekly market and 18th-century church.


### 5. Vague Attributions and Weasel Words

**Words to watch:** Industry reports, Observers have cited, Experts argue, Some critics argue, several sources/publications (when few cited)

**Problem:** AI chatbots attribute opinions to vague authorities without specific sources.

**Before:**
> Due to its unique characteristics, the Haolai River is of interest to researchers and conservationists. Experts believe it plays a crucial role in the regional ecosystem.

**After:**
> The Haolai River supports several endemic fish species, according to a 2019 survey by the Chinese Academy of Sciences.


### 6. Outline-like "Challenges and Future Prospects" Sections

**Words to watch:** Despite its... faces several challenges..., Despite these challenges, Challenges and Legacy, Future Outlook

**Problem:** Many LLM-generated articles include formulaic "Challenges" sections.

**Before:**
> Despite its industrial prosperity, Korattur faces challenges typical of urban areas, including traffic congestion and water scarcity. Despite these challenges, with its strategic location and ongoing initiatives, Korattur continues to thrive as an integral part of Chennai's growth.

**After:**
> Traffic congestion increased after 2015 when three new IT parks opened. The municipal corporation began a stormwater drainage project in 2022 to address recurring floods.


## LANGUAGE AND GRAMMAR PATTERNS

### 7. Overused "AI Vocabulary" Words

**High-frequency AI words:** Additionally, align with, crucial, delve, emphasizing, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, highlight (verb), interplay, intricate/intricacies, key (adjective), landscape (abstract noun), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract noun), testament, underscore (verb), valuable, vibrant

**Problem:** These words appear far more frequently in post-2023 text. They often co-occur.

**Before:**
> Additionally, a distinctive feature of Somali cuisine is the incorporation of camel meat. An enduring testament to Italian colonial influence is the widespread adoption of pasta in the local culinary landscape, showcasing how these dishes have integrated into the traditional diet.

**After:**
> Somali cuisine also includes camel meat, which is considered a delicacy. Pasta dishes, introduced during Italian colonization, remain common, especially in the south.


### 8. Avoidance of "is"/"are" (Copula Avoidance)

**Words to watch:** serves as/stands as/marks/represents [a], boasts/features/offers [a]

**Problem:** LLMs substitute elaborate constructions for simple copulas.

**Before:**
> Gallery 825 serves as LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery features four separate spaces and boasts over 3,000 square feet.

**After:**
> Gallery 825 is LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery has four rooms totaling 3,000 square feet.


### 9. Negative Parallelisms

**Problem:** Constructions like "Not only...but..." or "It's not just about..., it's..." are overused.

**Before:**
> It's not just about the beat riding under the vocals; it's part of the aggression and atmosphere. It's not merely a song, it's a statement.

**After:**
> The heavy beat adds to the aggressive tone.


### 10. Rule of Three Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs force ideas into groups of three to appear comprehensive.

**Before:**
> The event features keynote sessions, panel discussions, and networking opportunities. Attendees can expect innovation, inspiration, and industry insights.

**After:**
> The event includes talks and panels. There's also time for informal networking between sessions.


### 11. Elegant Variation (Synonym Cycling)

**Problem:** AI has repetition-penalty code causing excessive synonym substitution.

**Before:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges. The main character must overcome obstacles. The central figure eventually triumphs. The hero returns home.

**After:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges but eventually triumphs and returns home.


### 12. False Ranges

**Problem:** LLMs use "from X to Y" constructions where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale.

**Before:**
> Our journey through the universe has taken us from the singularity of the Big Bang to the grand cosmic web, from the birth and death of stars to the enigmatic dance of dark matter.

**After:**
> The book covers the Big Bang, star formation, and current theories about dark matter.


## STYLE PATTERNS

### 13. Em Dash Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs use em dashes (—) more than humans, mimicking "punchy" sales writing.

**Before:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions—not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address—yet this mislabeling continues—even in official documents.

**After:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions, not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address, yet this mislabeling continues in official documents.


### 14. Overuse of Boldface

**Problem:** AI chatbots emphasize phrases in boldface mechanically.

**Before:**
> It blends **OKRs (Objectives and Key Results)**, **KPIs (Key Performance Indicators)**, and visual strategy tools such as the **Business Model Canvas (BMC)** and **Balanced Scorecard (BSC)**.

**After:**
> It blends OKRs, KPIs, and visual strategy tools like the Business Model Canvas and Balanced Scorecard.


### 15. Inline-Header Vertical Lists

**Problem:** AI outputs lists where items start with bolded headers followed by colons.

**Before:**
> - **User Experience:** The user experience has been significantly improved with a new interface.
> - **Performance:** Performance has been enhanced through optimized algorithms.
> - **Security:** Security has been strengthened with end-to-end encryption.

**After:**
> The update improves the interface, speeds up load times through optimized algorithms, and adds end-to-end encryption.


### 16. Title Case in Headings

**Problem:** AI chatbots capitalize all main words in headings.

**Before:**
> ## Strategic Negotiations And Global Partnerships

**After:**
> ## Strategic negotiations and global partnerships


### 17. Emojis

**Problem:** AI chatbots often decorate headings or bullet points with emojis.

**Before:**
> 🚀 **Launch Phase:** The product launches in Q3
> 💡 **Key Insight:** Users prefer simplicity
> ✅ **Next Steps:** Schedule follow-up meeting

**After:**
> The product launches in Q3. User research showed a preference for simplicity. Next step: schedule a follow-up meeting.


### 18. Curly Quotation Marks

**Problem:** ChatGPT uses curly quotes (“...”) instead of straight quotes ("...").

**Before:**
> He said “the project is on track” but others disagreed.

**After:**
> He said "the project is on track" but others disagreed.


## COMMUNICATION PATTERNS

### 19. Collaborative Communication Artifacts

**Words to watch:** I hope this helps, Of course!, Certainly!, You're absolutely right!, Would you like..., let me know, here is a...

**Problem:** Text meant as chatbot correspondence gets pasted as content.

**Before:**
> Here is an overview of the French Revolution. I hope this helps! Let me know if you'd like me to expand on any section.

**After:**
> The French Revolution began in 1789 when financial crisis and food shortages led to widespread unrest.


### 20. Knowledge-Cutoff Disclaimers

**Words to watch:** as of [date], Up to my last training update, While specific details are limited/scarce..., based on available information...

**Problem:** AI disclaimers about incomplete information get left in text.

**Before:**
> While specific details about the company's founding are not extensively documented in readily available sources, it appears to have been established sometime in the 1990s.

**After:**
> The company was founded in 1994, according to its registration documents.


### 21. Sycophantic/Servile Tone

**Problem:** Overly positive, people-pleasing language.

**Before:**
> Great question! You're absolutely right that this is a complex topic. That's an excellent point about the economic factors.

**After:**
> The economic factors you mentioned are relevant here.


## FILLER AND HEDGING

### 22. Filler Phrases

**Before → After:**
- "In order to achieve this goal" → "To achieve this"
- "Due to the fact that it was raining" → "Because it was raining"
- "At this point in time" → "Now"
- "In the event that you need help" → "If you need help"
- "The system has the ability to process" → "The system can process"
- "It is important to note that the data shows" → "The data shows"


### 23. Excessive Hedging

**Problem:** Over-qualifying statements.

**Before:**
> It could potentially possibly be argued that the policy might have some effect on outcomes.

**After:**
> The policy may affect outcomes.


### 24. Generic Positive Conclusions

**Problem:** Vague upbeat endings.

**Before:**
> The future looks bright for the company. Exciting times lie ahead as they continue their journey toward excellence. This represents a major step in the right direction.

**After:**
> The company plans to open two more locations next year.


### 25. Hyphenated Word Pair Overuse

**Words to watch:** third-party, cross-functional, client-facing, data-driven, decision-making, well-known, high-quality, real-time, long-term, end-to-end

**Problem:** AI hyphenates common word pairs with perfect consistency. Humans rarely hyphenate these uniformly, and when they do, it's inconsistent. Less common or technical compound modifiers are fine to hyphenate.

**Before:**
> The cross-functional team delivered a high-quality, data-driven report on our client-facing tools. Their decision-making process was well-known for being thorough and detail-oriented.

**After:**
> The cross functional team delivered a high quality, data driven report on our client facing tools. Their decision making process was known for being thorough and detail oriented.

---

## Process

1. Read the input text carefully
2. Identify all instances of the patterns above
3. Rewrite each problematic section
4. Ensure the revised text:
   - Sounds natural when read aloud
   - Varies sentence structure naturally
   - Uses specific details over vague claims
   - Maintains appropriate tone for context
   - Uses simple constructions (is/are/has) where appropriate
5. Present a draft humanized version
6. Prompt: "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?"
7. Answer briefly with the remaining tells (if any)
8. Prompt: "Now make it not obviously AI generated."
9. Present the final version (revised after the audit)

## Output Format

Provide:
1. Draft rewrite
2. "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?" (brief bullets)
3. Final rewrite
4. A brief summary of changes made (optional, if helpful)


## Full Example

**Before (AI-sounding):**
> Great question! Here is an essay on this topic. I hope this helps!
>
> AI-assisted coding serves as an enduring testament to the transformative potential of large language models, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of software development. In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, these groundbreaking tools—nestled at the intersection of research and practice—are reshaping how engineers ideate, iterate, and deliver, underscoring their vital role in modern workflows.
>
> At its core, the value proposition is clear: streamlining processes, enhancing collaboration, and fostering alignment. It's not just about autocomplete; it's about unlocking creativity at scale, ensuring that organizations can remain agile while delivering seamless, intuitive, and powerful experiences to users. The tool serves as a catalyst. The assistant functions as a partner. The system stands as a foundation for innovation.
>
> Industry observers have noted that adoption has accelerated from hobbyist experiments to enterprise-wide rollouts, from solo developers to cross-functional teams. The technology has been featured in The New York Times, Wired, and The Verge. Additionally, the ability to generate documentation, tests, and refactors showcases how AI can contribute to better outcomes, highlighting the intricate interplay between automation and human judgment.
>

Eric

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence (commit+push to KeystoneOS is standing-authorized per `feedback-auto-commit-push`; for any OTHER repo with changes, commit locally and list the push as an open item instead of pushing).

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` in every repo touched this session (check cwd first, then any repo mentioned in the conversation; if session context is thin, check `KeystoneOS` and any `DEV/` repo with commits dated today).
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- KeystoneOS: stage, commit with a descriptive message, push. Authorized.
- Other repos with changes: commit locally with a descriptive message; do NOT push without asking — list it in the final report instead.
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Never push to a repo other than KeystoneOS without explicit approval.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

name: gws-forms-api
description: gws CLI can create and populate Google Forms with only the drive scope — no forms.body scope needed; create is title-only, items require batchUpdate
metadata:
  type: project
---

The `gws` CLI (`/opt/homebrew/bin/gws`, personal account eric.rash11@gmail.com) can
create and fully populate Google Forms even though **no `forms.body` scope is
granted**. The 12 granted scopes include `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive`,
and that is sufficient for both `forms forms create` and `forms forms batchUpdate`.

**Why:** worth recording because the Contacts API on this same auth returns 403 for a
missing scope (see [[fireflies-cli-broken-on-mac]] for the sibling env traps), so the
reasonable expectation is that Forms would fail too. It doesn't. Don't skip Forms work
on a scope assumption — try it.

**How to apply:**

- `gws forms forms create --json '{"info":{"title":"...","documentTitle":"..."}}'`
  accepts **title only**. The API rejects description, items, and settings on create.
- Everything else goes through `forms forms batchUpdate` with a `requests` array:
  `updateFormInfo` (with `updateMask`) for the description, then `createItem` with an
  incrementing `location.index` per question.
- Item shapes: `questionItem.question.textQuestion{paragraph:bool}`,
  `...choiceQuestion{type: RADIO|CHECKBOX|DROP_DOWN, options:[{value}]}`,
  and `pageBreakItem` for a section.
- Editing an existing question needs `updateItem` with the item's `itemId`, the
  question's `questionId`, `location.index`, **and** an `updateMask` such as
  `questionItem.question.choiceQuestion.options`. Omitting itemId/questionId appends a
  duplicate instead of editing in place.
- `--dry-run` validates locally before sending. Use it; batchUpdate is not idempotent
  and a re-run duplicates every item.
- New forms are created **published and accepting responses**. On a personal account
  that is a loose end — unpublish or delete after use.
- Gmail drafts work the same way via `gmail users drafts create/update` with a
  base64url RFC822 `message.raw`. Passing an existing draft `id` to `update` edits in
  place rather than creating a duplicate.

name: fireflies-cli-broken-on-mac
description: "fireflies-pp-cli's misleading \"out of memory (14)\" error means the local DB was never synced — not a real failure"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project

---

**Resolved 2026-08-11.** Recording the trap because the error message points the wrong way.

`fireflies-pp-cli` failed on **every** command and every `--data-source` (including
`live`) with:

```
Error: querying: unable to open database file: out of memory (14)
```

"Out of memory" is wrong — SQLite 14 is `SQLITE_CANTOPEN`. The real cause: the local
mirror had **never been created on this Mac**. Two things were missing after the
Windows → Mac migration:

1. No `FIREFLIES_API_KEY` anywhere — not env, not disk, not Keychain.
2. No database. `sync` had never been run here.

**`--data-source live` does not bypass the database.** Read commands open it regardless,
so "live" fails identically until a sync exists. That is what makes the error so
misleading — it looks like a corrupt/locked DB rather than a missing one.

**Fix:** `export FIREFLIES_API_KEY=...` in `~/.zshrc`, then `fireflies-pp-cli sync`.
Synced 189 transcripts / 200 records on first run.

**The DB lives at `~/.local/share/fireflies-pp-cli/data.db`** (XDG data dir), *not*
`~/.fireflies-pp-cli/` — that directory exists but stays empty and is a red herring.

**Shell gotcha:** `~/.zshrc` exports are invisible to Claude Code's Bash tool (it runs
non-interactive bash and does not source zshrc). Load them explicitly per command:
`eval "$(grep -m1 '^[[:space:]]*export[[:space:]]\+VARNAME' ~/.zshrc)"`

**Knock-on effect worth remembering:** `meeting-sync` hard-stops on auth failure and
`weekly-review` calls it first, so this single missing credential silently disabled both
rituals. The vault meeting corpus froze at 2026-08-03 and `Inbox/weekly-review/` went
empty after 2026-07-31. A lapse that reads as a discipline problem was a missing env var.
Design rule: recurring skills must **degrade and report staleness**, never hard-stop.

## Transcript text requires `--live` (added 2026-08-13)

`transcripts get <id>` returns metadata, speakers, and the AI summary but **no
`sentences` array** — and neither does the local DB (`json_extract(data,'$.sentences')`
is null) nor `transcripts export`, which emits only the summary (~2.6 KB).

To get the actual dialogue, add `--live`:

```
fireflies-pp-cli transcripts get <id> --live --json
```

That returned 476 sentences / 284 KB for a 39-minute meeting, vs 6 KB without it. So
`sync` does **not** mirror transcript bodies — only metadata and summaries. Plan any
transcript-reading work around one `--live` call, then condense locally (group

name: fireflies-cli-broken-on-mac
description: "fireflies-pp-cli's misleading \"out of memory (14)\" error means the local DB was never synced — not a real failure"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

**Resolved 2026-08-11.** Recording the trap because the error message points the wrong way.

`fireflies-pp-cli` failed on **every** command and every `--data-source` (including
`live`) with:

```
Error: querying: unable to open database file: out of memory (14)
```

"Out of memory" is wrong — SQLite 14 is `SQLITE_CANTOPEN`. The real cause: the local
mirror had **never been created on this Mac**. Two things were missing after the
Windows → Mac migration:

1. No `FIREFLIES_API_KEY` anywhere — not env, not disk, not Keychain.
2. No database. `sync` had never been run here.

**`--data-source live` does not bypass the database.** Read commands open it regardless,
so "live" fails identically until a sync exists. That is what makes the error so
misleading — it looks like a corrupt/locked DB rather than a missing one.

**Fix:** `export FIREFLIES_API_KEY=...` in `~/.zshrc`, then `fireflies-pp-cli sync`.
Synced 189 transcripts / 200 records on first run.

**The DB lives at `~/.local/share/fireflies-pp-cli/data.db`** (XDG data dir), *not*
`~/.fireflies-pp-cli/` — that directory exists but stays empty and is a red herring.

**Shell gotcha:** `~/.zshrc` exports are invisible to Claude Code's Bash tool (it runs
non-interactive bash and does not source zshrc). Load them explicitly per command:
`eval "$(grep -m1 '^[[:space:]]*export[[:space:]]\+VARNAME' ~/.zshrc)"`

**Knock-on effect worth remembering:** `meeting-sync` hard-stops on auth failure and
`weekly-review` calls it first, so this single missing credential silently disabled both
rituals. The vault meeting corpus froze at 2026-08-03 and `Inbox/weekly-review/` went
empty after 2026-07-31. A lapse that reads as a discipline problem was a missing env var.
Design rule: recurring skills must **degrade and report staleness**, never hard-stop.

# Handoff — ATH Technology Framework: post-meeting routing sheet + inventory

**Date:** 2026-08-13
**Owner:** Eric Rash (Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics)
**Predecessor:** `2026-08-12-ath-tech-software-framework.md` (the merge/build session)
**Status:** Meeting held 8/13 4:16 PM. Direction changed. Four new deliverables built,
two Google Forms live, one Gmail draft staged.

---

## What happened

The 8/13 "INITIAL DISCUSSION: ATH Technology/Software Review" meeting took place
(39.5 min, 7 speakers). Full transcript reviewed via
`fireflies-pp-cli transcripts get 01KZYFQ9F92NHG57AHSQJ2DFR4 --live`.

**The direction changed.** Micah Lamb (ITS) is writing a **counter-proposal**. He
likes the content but does not want a process running parallel to the university's
existing workflow:

> "I really don't think we need to go that far… if we instead had a more standardized
> intake and a more standardized framework around the requests coming from athletics,
> that would really streamline and speed up the path through the existing process.
> That's where I think we will see most of our gain for less effort."

Kenny Boyd then gave follow-up direction: build a **simple internal athletics routing
document** — yes/no logic, keyed on data type, Business Office as first layer, simple
enough to show ITS that review happens inside Athletics before requests reach them.
Separately: get a real **technology inventory**, and set a **standing meeting with
Micah**.

## Key decisions and the reasoning that would otherwise be lost

1. **The routing sheet outputs the settled Levels rather than competing with §6.**
   Three yes/no questions produce Level 1/2/3 as already defined. This answers Kenny
   (simple) and Micah (no parallel process) simultaneously, and keeps one definition of
   the levels instead of two. Truth table verified: all 8 combinations map to exactly
   one level, zero mismatches vs §6.

2. **Data type sets the floor; cost can only raise the level.** Pre-meeting analysis
   found zero-cost tools are the highest-risk, lowest-friction entry point — the
   Business Office filters on budget/contract/duplication and a free app has none of
   the three. This rule stops a free trial from downgrading an athlete-data request.

3. **The sheet says "before an IDEA form *or* a TCM request."** Erin Boyette raised
   that a request can complete the entire IT review before the Business Office sees it,
   because the Business Office only appears at the contract stage where TCM requires an
   IT project ID (added by Procurement without ITS's knowledge). Naming both entry
   points closes that gap.

4. **Plain language over §2.4 definitions.** "Physiologic" was replaced with "anything
   about an athlete's body, health, injury, or recovery." Micah's central complaint was
   that different people call the same data different things; formal definitions would
   reproduce the problem.

5. **Two inventory forms, not one.** A 5-question Quick Inventory for breadth, and the
   17-question Detailed Inventory as a targeted second pass. Asking 17 questions per
   product up front would suppress response rate.

6. **Microsoft Forms is the collection platform**; the Google Forms are scaffolds only.
   Collecting an inventory of athlete-data systems via a personal Google account would
   work against the project's own premise.

7. **Humanizer applied as pattern-removal only.** The skill's "add soul / first person
   / let some mess in" half is blog advice and would damage a staff email CC'ing Kenny
   and Jovon. Same call as the 8/12 session made on the framework doc.

## Files created this session

All under `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework/docs/`:

- `TALKING_POINTS_ER_2026-08-13_internal.md` — pre-meeting; shareable block + prep notes
- `MEETING_RECORD_2026-08-13_tech-software-review.md` — full transcript synthesis
- `ROUTING_ONEPAGER_ATH_2026-08-13.md` — **the core deliverable**
- `INVENTORY_FORM_SPEC_2026-08-13.md` — 17-question Microsoft Forms build spec
- `INVENTORY_EMAIL_DRAFT_2026-08-13.md` — distribution email (humanized)
- `INVENTORY_FORMS_LINKS.md` — both form URLs + shared 26-option department list
- `MICAH_MEETING_REQUEST_2026-08-13.md` — meeting request + standing-meeting agenda

Memory files written:
- `~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/project_gws-forms-api.md` (new)
- `.../project_fireflies-cli-broken-on-mac.md` (appended: `--live` requirement)

**Nothing was changed in `deliverables/`.** The merged framework docx is untouched —
Micah's counter-proposal is coming and editing now means editing twice.

## Live external state

- **Google Form — Quick Inventory** (5 q):
  `16gu5e962Iuyun-cyVTg4vxXlW2tLw5MngjcXMALRIxA`
- **Google Form — Detailed Inventory** (17 q):
  `1qVAdjmDs0uNGz1pV-1Nzdb6sEHx7RxL6MQmZd1pHsks`
- Both on the **personal** Google account, both **published and accepting responses**.
  Unpublish or delete once transferred to Microsoft Forms.
- **Gmail draft** `r-1535866246841293577` — inventory request email, To/Cc empty,
  personal account. Copy to Baylor mail before sending.

## Next actions, most important first

1. **Confirm the one open routing question.** The sheet routes *every* request to the
   Business Office first. Kenny's phrasing conditioned that on student-athlete data
   ("seems to be"). If Level 1 no-athlete-data requests should skip straight to the
   IDEA form, it's a one-line change to Step 3.
2. **Schedule the Micah meeting** before his counter-proposal is final, so the two
   documents converge instead of competing. Draft text is in
   `MICAH_MEETING_REQUEST_2026-08-13.md`. Worth raising in that meeting: framework §1.7
   already specified the weekly ITS standing meeting Kenny independently asked for.
3. **Rebuild the Quick Inventory in Microsoft Forms**, add recipients, send from Baylor
   mail with Kenny + Jovon on CC. Suggested deadline Fri Aug 29 (adjust for fall camp).
4. **Then** report out to Cody Hall and Jovon Overshown per Kenny's instruction.
5. Unpublish/delete the two Google Forms after transfer.

## Still open from pre-meeting analysis — not discussed on 8/13

These were found in the framework and remain unaddressed:
- **Trials/pilots:** Form 1 offers "Provisional / trial" and the Scorecard offers
  "Approve as trial with hard end date," but the framework body has zero occurrences of
  trial/pilot/demo (§8.2 was cut on Aug 11; the forms are dated Aug 4 and were never
  revised). Decide: restore a short section, or strip the option from the forms.

# Athletics Technology Request — Routing Sheet

**Internal to Athletics. Complete this before submitting an ITS IDEA form or a TCM
contract request.** One page, three questions. It tells you who needs to look at a
request inside Athletics, and it produces a short record that travels with the
request to ITS.

---

## Step 1 — Three questions

**1. Does it collect, store, or display any information about a student-athlete?**
*Names, rosters, video of athletes, performance numbers, survey answers — anything
tied to an individual athlete.*
☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Not sure

**2. Does it involve anything about an athlete's body, health, injury, or recovery —
or will athlete information leave Baylor or be handled by an outside company?**
*Sleep, wellness surveys, GPS or load monitoring, force plate, heart rate, injury or
medical notes, rehab or return-to-play status. Also yes if the vendor stores or
processes the data on their own systems.*
☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Not sure

**3. Is there a recurring cost, or will more than one team or unit use it?**
☐ Yes  ☐ No  ☐ Not sure

> **"Not sure" counts as Yes.** And data type sets the floor — a free trial, a
> donated license, or a low one-time price never lowers the level.

## Step 2 — Read the level

| If | Level |
|---|---|
| Question 2 is Yes | **Level 3 — Comprehensive Review** |
| Question 2 is No, but Question 1 is Yes | **Level 2 — Enhanced Review** |
| Questions 1 and 2 are No, but Question 3 is Yes | **Level 2 — Enhanced Review** |
| All three are No | **Level 1 — Standard Review** |

## Step 3 — Route it

**Every request starts with the Business Office** — funding, duplication, and whether
Athletics already owns something that does this.

| Level | Route |
|---|---|
| **1 — Standard** | Business Office → ITS IDEA form |
| **2 — Enhanced** | Business Office → Applied Performance + requesting unit → ITS IDEA form |
| **3 — Comprehensive** | Business Office → Applied Performance + Health & Wellness / Sports Medicine sign-off → ITS IDEA form |

## Step 4 — Athletics Review Record

*Paste or attach this to the IDEA form submission. This is what shows ITS the request
was reviewed inside Athletics before it reached them.*

```
Product / platform:
Requested by (name, sport or unit):
Problem it solves:
Existing solution checked?      ☐ Yes — which: ____________   ☐ No
Data involved:   ☐ None   ☐ Athlete performance   ☐ Health / medical
                 ☐ Leaves Baylor or vendor-processed
Level assigned:  ☐ 1   ☐ 2   ☐ 3
Business Office reviewed by / date:
Athletics review by / date:
Vendor information obtained:  ☐ Security documentation
                              ☐ Data export & deletion terms
                              ☐ Pricing and contract term
```

---

## Notes — not part of the sheet

**Why it is built this way.** Micah Lamb's stated objection to the full framework was
that it creates a process parallel to the university's existing workflow. This sheet
does not. It is a front door: it produces better-formed requests entering the existing
IDEA form process, which is what he asked for. Two things he named as the biggest
sources of delay — nobody declaring what data is involved, and nobody knowing whether
the rest of Athletics is aware — are answered by Step 4.

**Why it says "before an IDEA form *or* a TCM request."** Erin Boyette raised that a
request can complete the entire IT review before the Business Office ever sees it,
because the Business Office only appears at the contract stage where TCM requires an
IT project ID. Naming both entry points is what closes that gap.

**The levels are the settled ones.** This sheet does not invent a new scheme — the
three questions just produce Level 1 / 2 / 3 as already defined in §6 of the
framework. The sheet is the simple front end; §6 remains the definition.

**Vendor information, Step 4.** Micah's point: vendors answer security and data
questions readily while they are still selling, and much less readily once they think
the sale is closed. Asking early is worth the thirty seconds.

# Handoff — ATH Technology Framework: post-meeting routing sheet + inventory

**Date:** 2026-08-13
**Owner:** Eric Rash (Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics)
**Predecessor:** `2026-08-12-ath-tech-software-framework.md` (the merge/build session)
**Status:** Meeting held 8/13 4:16 PM. Direction changed. Four new deliverables built,
two Google Forms live, one Gmail draft staged.

---

## What happened

The 8/13 "INITIAL DISCUSSION: ATH Technology/Software Review" meeting took place
(39.5 min, 7 speakers). Full transcript reviewed via
`fireflies-pp-cli transcripts get 01KZYFQ9F92NHG57AHSQJ2DFR4 --live`.

**The direction changed.** Micah Lamb (ITS) is writing a **counter-proposal**. He
likes the content but does not want a process running parallel to the university's
existing workflow:

> "I really don't think we need to go that far… if we instead had a more standardized
> intake and a more standardized framework around the requests coming from athletics,
> that would really streamline and speed up the path through the existing process.
> That's where I think we will see most of our gain for less effort."

Kenny Boyd then gave follow-up direction: build a **simple internal athletics routing
document** — yes/no logic, keyed on data type, Business Office as first layer, simple
enough to show ITS that review happens inside Athletics before requests reach them.
Separately: get a real **technology inventory**, and set a **standing meeting with
Micah**.

## Key decisions and the reasoning that would otherwise be lost

1. **The routing sheet outputs the settled Levels rather than competing with §6.**
   Three yes/no questions produce Level 1/2/3 as already defined. This answers Kenny
   (simple) and Micah (no parallel process) simultaneously, and keeps one definition of
   the levels instead of two. Truth table verified: all 8 combinations map to exactly
   one level, zero mismatches vs §6.

2. **Data type sets the floor; cost can only raise the level.** Pre-meeting analysis
   found zero-cost tools are the highest-risk, lowest-friction entry point — the
   Business Office filters on budget/contract/duplication and a free app has none of
   the three. This rule stops a free trial from downgrading an athlete-data request.

3. **The sheet says "before an IDEA form *or* a TCM request."** Erin Boyette raised
   that a request can complete the entire IT review before the Business Office sees it,
   because the Business Office only appears at the contract stage where TCM requires an
   IT project ID (added by Procurement without ITS's knowledge). Naming both entry
   points closes that gap.

4. **Plain language over §2.4 definitions.** "Physiologic" was replaced with "anything
   about an athlete's body, health, injury, or recovery." Micah's central complaint was
   that different people call the same data different things; formal definitions would
   reproduce the problem.

5. **Two inventory forms, not one.** A 5-question Quick Inventory for breadth, and the
   17-question Detailed Inventory as a targeted second pass. Asking 17 questions per
   product up front would suppress response rate.

6. **Microsoft Forms is the collection platform**; the Google Forms are scaffolds only.
   Collecting an inventory of athlete-data systems via a personal Google account would
   work against the project's own premise.

7. **Humanizer applied as pattern-removal only.** The skill's "add soul / first person
   / let some mess in" half is blog advice and would damage a staff email CC'ing Kenny
   and Jovon. Same call as the 8/12 session made on the framework doc.

## Files created this session

All under `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework/docs/`:

- `TALKING_POINTS_ER_2026-08-13_internal.md` — pre-meeting; shareable block + prep notes
- `MEETING_RECORD_2026-08-13_tech-software-review.md` — full transcript synthesis
- `ROUTING_ONEPAGER_ATH_2026-08-13.md` — **the core deliverable**
- `INVENTORY_FORM_SPEC_2026-08-13.md` — 17-question Microsoft Forms build spec
- `INVENTORY_EMAIL_DRAFT_2026-08-13.md` — distribution email (humanized)
- `INVENTORY_FORMS_LINKS.md` — both form URLs + shared 26-option department list
- `MICAH_MEETING_REQUEST_2026-08-13.md` — meeting request + standing-meeting agenda

Memory files written:
- `~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/project_gws-forms-api.md` (new)
- `.../project_fireflies-cli-broken-on-mac.md` (appended: `--live` requirement)

**Nothing was changed in `deliverables/`.** The merged framework docx is untouched —
Micah's counter-proposal is coming and editing now means editing twice.

## Live external state

- **Google Form — Quick Inventory** (5 q):
  `16gu5e962Iuyun-cyVTg4vxXlW2tLw5MngjcXMALRIxA`
- **Google Form — Detailed Inventory** (17 q):
  `1qVAdjmDs0uNGz1pV-1Nzdb6sEHx7RxL6MQmZd1pHsks`
- Both on the **personal** Google account, both **published and accepting responses**.
  Unpublish or delete once transferred to Microsoft Forms.
- **Gmail draft** `r-1535866246841293577` — inventory request email, To/Cc empty,
  personal account. Copy to Baylor mail before sending.

## Next actions, most important first

1. **Confirm the one open routing question.** The sheet routes *every* request to the
   Business Office first. Kenny's phrasing conditioned that on student-athlete data
   ("seems to be"). If Level 1 no-athlete-data requests should skip straight to the
   IDEA form, it's a one-line change to Step 3.
2. **Schedule the Micah meeting** before his counter-proposal is final, so the two
   documents converge instead of competing. Draft text is in
   `MICAH_MEETING_REQUEST_2026-08-13.md`. Worth raising in that meeting: framework §1.7
   already specified the weekly ITS standing meeting Kenny independently asked for.
3. **Rebuild the Quick Inventory in Microsoft Forms**, add recipients, send from Baylor
   mail with Kenny + Jovon on CC. Suggested deadline Fri Aug 29 (adjust for fall camp).
4. **Then** report out to Cody Hall and Jovon Overshown per Kenny's instruction.
5. Unpublish/delete the two Google Forms after transfer.

## Still open from pre-meeting analysis — not discussed on 8/13

These were found in the framework and remain unaddressed:
- **Trials/pilots:** Form 1 offers "Provisional / trial" and the Scorecard offers
  "Approve as trial with hard end date," but the framework body has zero occurrences of
  trial/pilot/demo (§8.2 was cut on Aug 11; the forms are dated Aug 4 and were never
  revised). Decide: restore a short section, or strip the option from the forms.
- **Student-Athlete Notice:** defined in §2.4, required nowhere. §3 claims the framework
  is Baylor's NCAA SSI implementation, where athlete transparency is central.
  (Note: Form 2's "notice" is *contract cancellation* notice — a different concept.)
- **Discontinuation:** Phase 3.4 can conclude "discontinue"; Procurement's role requires
  contracts to address retention/deletion/portability; no phase step executes either.
- **No effective date, transition plan, or bypass-detection mechanism.**

## Context worth carrying

- Kenny closed the meeting frustrated — nine years of hearing athletics systems can't
  connect with campus health and counseling, and he said the campus EMR investment
  doesn't solve athletics' problem. Temperature matters for follow-ups.
- Micah committed to adding the Athletics Business Office to IDEA form
  auto-notifications (can start immediately for athletics), a business-officer dropdown
  campus-wide by mid-fall, and optionally auto-looping Kenny's team on athlete-data
  requests. Confirm Athletics is in the first wave.
- Roughly 1,000 IDEA form requests came through last year (~3/day, clumped). Jon Allen
  warned against two serial processes turning a 2-week turnaround into 8–10 weeks —
  any defense of the framework must answer this.
- Bypass rate estimated at ~20% by Cody and Kenny. Quick-form question 11 ("did it go
  through the IDEA form?") is designed to measure it rather than estimate it.

message.content: in your opinion what is the best time to send him an email to follow up. We had the meeting yesterday and today is friday. Should I send it monday along with the email to the operations staff asking for the technology inventory?

content.text:
Don't bundle them. They're on completely different clocks, and one of them is genuinely urgent.

**Send Micah's today.** Here's the line that decides it — Micah, in the meeting:

> "What I'm going to do next after this meeting is kind of go through it and make a counter proposal of how I think we can do all of those things without creating a parallel framework or flow, **and send that to the same group.**"

"After this meeting" means he may be writing it right now, and Kenny closed with "look forward to seeing your markups." Once that counter-proposal hits the group, it becomes the anchor document and your routing sheet turns into a *response* to it. Right now your sheet can still be an *input*. That's a materially better position and it expires without warning — possibly today.

The email doesn't need a reply Friday. It needs to be sitting in his inbox before he hits send. Even if he reads it Monday, it lands before the counter-proposal is final, which is the entire function.

There's also a relationship argument for going now. Your routing sheet already concedes his central point — no parallel process. So the message is "I heard you, here's me acting on it," and that reads far better *before* he's sunk effort into a full counter-document than after. Waiting risks looking like you're reacting to his markups rather than having already moved.

**The inventory email shouldn't go Monday either.** Two reasons. It's blocked on the Microsoft Forms rebuild, which isn't done. And Monday morning is a bad slot for a broad ask to a busy list — it competes with the weekend inbox flush. Tuesday or Wednesday morning is the better window, which also gives you time to build the form properly.

So: **Micah today, inventory Tuesday or Wednesday.**

Two smaller things. Don't CC Kenny on the Micah email — he asked you to run the conversation and report back, so a direct note to Micah and a status update to Kenny afterward matches what he actually requested. And your Aug 29 deadline lands in football game-week prep during camp; I'd either accept that football ops comes in late or give them a separate verbal ask, rather than moving the date for everyone.

Micah,

Thanks for the read on the proposal yesterday, and for saying plainly where you think
it goes too far. That was useful.

and ITS on this. Would a recurring 30 minutes work for you — weekly to start, then we

to stop the ad-hoc ones from reaching you without context.

Let me know what works and I'll send the invite.

Eric

---

## Suggested agenda — first meeting (30 min)

| Time | Item |
|---|---|
| 0–5 | Where your counter-proposal is heading — listen first, don't present |
| 5–15 | Walk the routing sheet: three questions, the level it produces, the review record that travels with the IDEA form |
| 15–22 | The two ordering problems: requests that reach ITS before the Business Office, and the TCM / IT project ID sequence |
| 22–27 | The business-officer dropdown and athlete-data auto-notification he offered — confirm Athletics is in the first wave |
| 27–30 | Set the standing cadence |

**Go in listening.** He is writing a counter-proposal and has been generous about the
work so far. The routing sheet already concedes his central point, so lead with that
rather than defending the full framework — it's the fastest way to a shared document
instead of two competing ones.

## Standing meeting — proposed structure

Weekly, 30 minutes, Eric + Micah, with others pulled in as needed.

1. **Open requests** — status, and specifically what is blocked and on whom
2. **New requests since last week** — did each arrive with a completed review record
3. **Anything that arrived off-process** — how it got in, so the routing gets fixed
4. **One process item** — a single improvement per week rather than a standing debate

Then Eric reports out to Cody Hall, Jovon Overshown, and Kenny after each meeting, per
Kenny's instruction.

---

**§1.7 of the framework already specified this.** It calls for the Director of Applied
Performance to hold a weekly standing meeting with ITS covering all open requests
across all units, with requesters pulled in only when needed. Kenny arrived at the same
operating model independently, after the meeting, without reference to the document.

That's a genuine point in the framework's favor and it costs nothing to mention — it
shifts the conversation from "is this framework too much" toward "which parts of it
were right," which is the more useful argument to be having with him.
